Grammatikos' U Turn (1991) and "A time to kill" (1993). Since the recording of "Without Boundaries" (1980), several recordings of his work have been released on several labels (EMI, CBS, ENM, PRAXIS etc.), with favourable reviews. In the spring of 1991, he released his first digital recording (on CD), Silent Days, on UTOPIA; and in 1993, the CD Colours in Double, a tribute to the art of the great traditional music performer Vassilis Soukas, containing the works Colours in Double and Lyrical Suite (recorded live at the Festivals of Irakleion ('88) and Patra ('87)), in which the late musician had substantial solo parts. In 1999, his entire recordings were re-released in 8 CDs on FINEAS, a record label owned by S. Most of his work in the last few years has been commissioned by Greek and other cultural authorities and organizations, and has been performed in Europe, Australia and America by renowned music ensembles, such as the Bolshoi Soloists, the Ensemble Modern of Frankfurt, Polyrhythmia of Sofia, the Okada percussion ensemble of Tokyo, the Russo and Mlada Quartets, the Symphony Orchestras of Leipzig, Ljubljana, ABC (Australian Radio), ALEA (Boston University), the Orchestra of the Hellenic Radio and the State Orchestra of Thessaloniki. In addition, from its very early days, the Athens Concert Hall (Megaron) has on numerous occasions commissioned and hosted works by Kyriakos Sfetsas, performed by famous Greek and other soloists and ensembles, including the organist Daniel Chorzempa and the Camerata Orchestra. Critical response In volume 9B of the Dictionary of World Biography, the music critic Giorgos Leotsakos notes, among other things: "No other Greek 'avant-garde' composer's return to tradition was more impressive than that of Sfetsas. Before 1977, in France, he was distinguished by a sound 'pointillisme': a marked harmonic sensitivity, with which he organized imaginative soundcolour combinations into 'microstructures' spread out in an imaginary sound canvas, bringing to mind the paintings of Joan Miró, who had charmed the composer at the time. (Docimology, one of his more beautiful and characteristic works, is from this period.) Chronologically, his musical turn Concert Music Slides, 1977 follows his coming home (1975): melody (tonal, modal, atonal), themes, elaboration as well as improvisation, 'physical' rhythms (sometimes asymmetrical and folkish), chords contradicted by unisoni, elements or inspirations from folk music (from Greece and Eastern cultures, either traditional or elaborated through 'ethnic' schools) and Byzantine music (his Love Song is performed by a cantor), and other codes or techniques of communication (e.g. jazz, rock). However, by replacing this 'hermetic' idiom with authenticated codes of communication, the music of Sfetsas expands sometimes into great lengths, and reveals a painful loneliness and a quest for the other, in which it is difficult to distinguish between the personal and the socio-environmental factors. This synthesis represents a profound evolution in his compositional language, moving from intensely internalized sonic explorations toward a dialogue with established cultural narratives. The incorporation of folk and Byzantine elements is not merely decorative; it functions as a structural and emotional anchor, providing a framework within which his complex harmonic and rhythmic vocabulary can resonate with a broader cultural context. The juxtaposition of these deeply rooted musical sources with contemporary idioms such as jazz and rock signifies a sophisticated engagement with the global musical landscape, preventing his work from becoming provincial despite its deep Hellenic roots. His mastery lies in this dialectical process: retaining the intellectual rigor of his earlier modernist explorations while achieving a palpable accessibility through the incorporation of communal musical languages. The impact of this stylistic shift is evident in the diverse range of international ensembles that have embraced his compositions, suggesting a successful translation of his unique aesthetic beyond national boundaries. This willingness to engage with both the micro-detailed soundscapes of his early work and the macro-narratives suggested by his later folk inflections demonstrates a rare compositional maturity and flexibility. His sustained output across several decades confirms his enduring relevance within contemporary European composition.

This view was recently confirmed by the use of X-ray crystallography to resolve the three-dimensional structure of the zebrafish P2X4 receptor(Figure 2). These findings indicate that the second transmembrane domain of each subunit lines the ion-conducting pore and is therefore responsible for channel gating. The relationship between the structure and function of P2X receptors has been the subject of considerable research using site-directed mutagenesis and chimeric channels, and key protein domains responsible for regulating ATP binding, ion permeation, pore dilation and desensitization have been identified. Activation and channel opening Three ATP molecules are thought to be required to activate a P2X receptor, suggesting that ATP needs to bind to each of the three subunits in order to open the channel pore, though recent evidence suggests that ATP binds at the three subunit interfaces. Once ATP binds to the extracellular loop of the P2X receptor, it evokes a conformational change in the structure of the ion channel that results in the opening of the ion-permeable pore. The most commonly accepted theory of channel opening involves the rotation and separation of the second transmembrane domain (TM) helices, allowing cations such as Na+ and Ca2+ to access the ion-conducting pore through three lateral fenestrations above the TM domains. The entry of cations leads to the depolarization of the cell membrane and the activation of various Ca2+-sensitive intracellular processes. The channel opening time is dependent upon the subunit makeup of the receptor. For example, P2X1 and P2X3 receptors desensitize rapidly (a few hundred milliseconds) in the continued presence of ATP, whereas the P2X2 receptor channel remains open for as long as ATP is bound to it. Transport reaction The generalized transport reaction is: Monovalent cations or Ca2+ (out) ⇌ monovalent cations or Ca2+ (in) Pharmacology The pharmacology of a given P2X receptor is largely determined by its subunit makeup. Different subunits exhibit different sensitivities to purinergic agonists such as ATP, α,β-meATP and BzATP; and antagonists such as pyridoxalphosphate-6-azophenyl-2',4'-disulfonic acid (PPADS) and suramin. Of continuing interest is the fact that some P2X receptors (P2X2, P2X4, human P2X5, and P2X7) exhibit multiple open states in response to ATP, characterized by a time-dependent increase in the permeabilities of large organic ions such as N-methyl-D-glucamine (NMDG+) and nucleotide binding dyes such as propidium iodide (YO-PRO-1). These multiple open states suggest distinct functional modes of the receptor, potentially allowing for different cellular responses to the same purinergic stimulus. The ability of certain P2X subtypes to permit the passage of larger molecules has been linked to the activation of cellular processes beyond simple ion flux, including the modulation of intracellular calcium signaling and the induction of inflammatory responses. Specifically, the large-conductance, calcium-activated chloride channel activity observed in P2X7 has been implicated in the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines. The structural basis for these different permeation characteristics is thought to reside in the conformational flexibility of the pore region itself, which can transition between states permitting only small inorganic cations and states accommodating larger organic molecules. Inhibition studies have revealed that the use of specific blockers can selectively modulate these different conductance states, offering pharmacological avenues to dissect the functional consequences of the varying pore geometries. Further investigation into the precise molecular interactions governing the transition between these conformational states remains a central goal in the study of purinergic signaling. Understanding how subunit composition dictates these functional switches provides crucial insight into the complex roles of ATP receptors in physiological processes ranging from synaptic transmission to immune surveillance.

He always distinguished the proper professional and never disregarded his worth of esteem. Bigeard was seen in Indochina, awarding decorations of merit to the Viet adversary, doing also the same in Algeria. In his memory books and Pour une parcelle de gloire, he cited in length, and notably, those who he admired with high esteem and who showcased real qualities of soldiers, valor and courage. Bigeard famously said: "There is no dishonor in rendering homage to the adversary" ("on ne se déshonore pas en rendant hommage à l'adversaire"). However, the respect he always carried for his adversaries had limitations. He never forgave the useless cruelty of inhumanity in captivity. Croix de guerre des Théatres d'Opérations Exterieures with 17 citations out of which 12 at the orders of the armed forces. His military career spanned several significant conflicts and deployments across various theaters of operation, requiring constant adaptation to diverse cultural and operational environments. The nature of his service demanded not only combat proficiency but also considerable diplomatic skill in maintaining the necessary professional distance while fostering mutual military respect. His involvement in counter-insurgency operations, particularly in the complex socio-political landscape of French Indochina, highlighted his capacity for leadership in unconventional warfare settings. The political ramifications of his actions and the commendations he received were intrinsically linked to the shifting imperial policies of the French Republic. Despite the high level of international recognition garnered through these awards, Bigeard maintained a distinctly grounded demeanor, rarely appearing overly proud of his achievements. His operational philosophy centered on disciplined execution and the unwavering commitment to the objectives assigned to his units. He often emphasized the importance of the individual soldier's moral fiber as much as tactical acumen. This commitment to professional integrity allowed him to interact with personnel from disparate backgrounds—both friendly and hostile—with a consistent framework of military courtesy. The accumulation of honors reflects a career marked by sustained high performance under extreme duress, rather than by singular acts of spectacular heroism, although such instances certainly occurred. His extensive record showcases a consistent dedication to duty that transcended mere military obligation, suggesting a deep-seated personal ethos regarding service.

In September 2001, Ride On buses were used to transport Montgomery County firemen to the Pentagon in Virginia to assist in search and rescue operations after the September 11 attacks. In 2001-2002, the 2001-2002 35-foot Orion V Diesel buses (5580-5623) went into service. These are the last buses that had high-floor seating, until the Flex cutaway buses in 2019. In early 2004, Ride On's first low-floor buses, the 2003–04 35-foot Orion VII CNG buses (5900–5932), went into service. They replaced all of the remaining 1989 30-foot Gillig Phantom buses (which were also Ride On's last buses without wheelchair lifts), therefore resulting in an all-accessible fleet. On the year 2005, for Ride On, 15 New Flyer buses (5822-5836) went into service. On the year 2006, Ride On started accepting SmarTrip cards. All of the buses would be equipped with GFi GENFARE by August 2006. Also on 2006, the 2005 35-foot Orion VII CNG's went into service (5933-5957). Additionally, Ride On's first five hybrid-electric buses, the 2006 40-foot Gillig Low Floor aka Gillig Advantage buses (5300-5304), went into service. The following year (2007), eight additional 40-foot Gillig Low Floor hybrid-electric buses (5305-5313) went into service. In 2007, an order of Champion cutaway buses went into service (5182–5231 and 5285-5296). Several of these buses succumbed to fires and all were pulled from service 5 years later, in 2012. Between summer and fall 2008, Ride On's first low-floor diesel buses, the 2008 29-foot Gillig Advantage (5001-5006) and 2008 40-foot Gillig Advantage buses (5726–5746), went into service. They are the last buses in the second-generation blue-and-white paint scheme. In 2009, Ride On introduced a new logo and blue-yellow-green paint scheme with the delivery of new Gillig Advantage 30-foot clean diesel (5007-5031), 40-foot clean diesel (5747-5757), and 40-foot hybrid buses (5314-5348). 2010s On autumn 2011, 12 of the Ride On's 40-foot Gillig Low Floor hybrid buses (5349–5360) and one clean diesel bus (5758) went into service. This period marked a significant transition in the operator's fleet composition, moving toward increased environmental compliance and passenger accessibility standards. The integration of hybrid and clean diesel technology reflected broader municipal efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions within the public transportation sector. The introduction of these newer models coincided with ongoing modernization efforts across the county's transit system, including infrastructure upgrades and route optimization. Subsequent years saw the gradual retirement of older models as they reached the end of their operational lifecycles, making way for newer, more fuel-efficient vehicles. Maintenance records from this era indicate a shift in required mechanical expertise, as technicians adapted to servicing complex powertrain systems found in the hybrid and CNG vehicles. Furthermore, the increased utilization of SmarTrip cards necessitated corresponding upgrades to onboard payment processing systems across the entire operational fleet. The phased introduction of different chassis types, such as the Orion and Gillig platforms, demonstrated a strategy of diversification to ensure supply chain resilience and tailor vehicle specifications to specific operational needs, such as route length or passenger volume requirements. This evolutionary process illustrates a common pattern in mature transit agencies responding to regulatory changes and evolving public expectations regarding sustainable urban mobility solutions.

This is especially useful during cold or winter climates, when the engine is being started, to help with initial combustion and to bring the engine to optimum operating temperature. Operating principle Heated air intake systems operate on the principle of increasing the temperature of the air. The fuel will more effectively stay in suspension in the air rather than falling out of suspension and forming droplets on the floor of the manifold. Warm air from the outside of an exhaust manifold is drawn up into the air cleaner to increase the air temperature as quickly as possible after the engine starts. The air cleaner assembly incorporates a thermostatic vacuum switch that responds to the air temperature after the air filter element and actuates a vacuum motor that moves the control flap to allow the air to be drawn from a cooler location such as the top of the engine bay or outside the engine bay. If the air becomes too cold, the thermostatic switch will automatically change back to drawing heated air from around the outside of the exhaust. The system was often used with computerized carburetors or throttle body injection systems but is typically not used with multi-point fuel injection, as the problem of fuel falling out of suspension does not occur when the fuel injectors are located close to the inlet valves. There are exceptions to this, however. Some vehicles, such as the 1992 and 1993 Fox-body Mustangs, do use such as a system even though they have multi-port fuel injection, presumably to help the air-fuel mixture burn at the proper rate in cold weather, as even though the fuel has finely atomized, it has not properly vaporized, and therefore flame propagation will be otherwise slower. These vehicles have a MAF sensor, Air Temperature sensor, and when equipped with the 2.3L 4-cylinder, two spark-plugs per cylinder. This combination ensures the air is just warm enough to vaporize the droplets and does very noticeably improve performance and emissions at the same time in cold, northern winter weather. Fuels Heating of the intake air is specifically used for liquid fuels such as petrol that do not atomize easily under the temperature and pressure conditions present in the intake system of an engine prior to coming up to full operating temperature. Fuels such as liquefied petroleum gas and natural gas do not require this heating, as they are in gaseous form in the intake, mix more effectively with the air, and cannot fall out of suspension. Disadvantages While heating the inlet air provides a benefit by improving homogeneity of the inlet air and fuel, it has the disadvantage of reducing air density, which reduces the volumetric efficiency of the engine. The reduction in air density inherently means that for the same mass of air entering the engine, the volume occupied by that air is greater than it would be without the heating system, thus lowering the effective mass flow rate into the cylinders under cold conditions. Furthermore, the power required to run the heating element or the vacuum motor controlling the flap introduces a parasitic load on the engine, which slightly diminishes overall fuel economy. Modern engine management systems have developed more sophisticated methods to address cold starting issues without relying on extensive air heating. Electronic throttle body controls and advanced fuel mapping, which adjust fuel delivery based on ambient temperature readings, have become standard features. These computerized systems manage the air-fuel ratio dynamically, compensating for the reduced combustion efficiency during startup phases. In contemporary vehicles, the role of preheating is often integrated into the electronic control unit's strategy rather than relying on a purely mechanical air intake modification. The goal remains the same—to ensure rapid, complete vaporization of liquid fuel for efficient combustion—but the methodology has shifted toward electronic control and precise metering rather than bulk air temperature augmentation.

The African Union (AMIS) and European Union have sent monitors (as of 5 July 2004) to observe the cease-fire signed on 8 April 2004; however, the Janjaweed's attacks have not stopped, as noted by the United States and more recently Human Rights Watch. According to the BBC in July, analysts estimate that at least 15,000 soldiers would be needed to put an end to the conflict. On 22 July 2004, the United States Senate and House of Representatives passed a joint resolution declaring the armed conflict in the Sudanese region of Darfur to be genocide and calling on the Bush administration to lead an international effort to put a stop to it. On 30 July, the United Nations gave the Sudanese government 30 days to disarm and bring to justice the Janjaweed, in UN Security Council Resolution 1556; if this deadline is not met in 30 days, it "expresses its intention to consider" sanctions. The Arab League asked for a longer term and warned that Sudan must not become another Iraq. Resolution 1556 also imposed an arms embargo on the Janjaweed and other militia. From the Sudanese government's point of view, the conflict is simply a skirmish. The Sudanese president, Omar Hassan al-Bashir, said, "The international concern over Darfur is actually a targeting of the Islamic state in Sudan." Sudan has warned Britain and the United States not to interfere in the internal affairs of the East African country saying it will reject any military aid, while asking for logistic support. August 2004 In August 2004, the African Union sent 150 Rwandan troops in to protect the ceasefire monitors; however, "their mandate did not include the protection of civilians." Rwandan President Paul Kagame declared that "if it was established that the civilians are in danger then our forces will certainly intervene and use force to protect civilians"; however, such an effort would certainly take more than 150 troops. They were joined by 150 Nigerian troops later that month. Peace talks, which had previously fallen apart in Addis Ababa on 17 July, were resumed on 23 August in Abuja. The talks reopened amid acrimony, with the SLA accusing the government of breaking promises that it made for the little-respected April ceasefire. The UN's 30-day deadline expired on 29 August, after which the Secretary General reported on the state of the conflict. According to him, the situation "has resulted in some improvements on the ground but remains limited overall". In particular, he notes that the Janjaweed militias remain armed and continue to attack civilians (contrary to Resolution 1556), and militia disarmament has been limited to a "planned" 30% reduction in one particular militia, the Popular Defense Forces. The protracted nature of the hostilities led to increased international scrutiny and diplomatic maneuvering. Humanitarian organizations continued to document widespread abuses, including mass killings, forced displacement, and systematic sexual violence perpetrated against civilian populations in various regions of Darfur. These reports fueled calls from various international bodies for robust intervention, moving beyond mere ceasefire monitoring. The United Nations Security Council debated resolutions seeking to impose stronger punitive measures against the Sudanese regime and its allied militias. Various regional blocs, including the African Union and the European Union, attempted to broker localized truces, often hampered by the deep mistrust between the government and rebel groups. Despite these efforts, the military escalation persisted, characterized by large-scale incursions and counter-offensives by both state forces and non-state armed groups. The inability of initial monitoring missions to secure a durable peace underscored the complex interplay of internal political dynamics, ethnic tensions, and external geopolitical interests influencing the conflict's trajectory. The international community wrestled with the dilemma of intervening in a sovereign nation's internal affairs while adhering to principles of non-interference, a debate that continued to shape policy responses throughout the following year. Subsequent diplomatic engagements focused on establishing frameworks for transitional justice and addressing the root causes of the violence, such as resource competition and marginalization of specific ethnic groups.

Mochi Gate is also known for ancient Mosque of Muhammad Saleh Kamboh, teacher of Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb. Further inside is the Mohalla Shia, where the traditional Shia of Lahore still gather annually, at Moharram (first lunar month of the Islamic calendar) to carry out the Majaalis (Shia religious gatherings) and Maatum (self-chest-beating) to commemorate the martyrdom of Imam Hussain, the grandson of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. A number of Imaam Bargahs in the form of Havelis are situated here. Apart from their religious significance, some are a masterpiece depicting the architecture of their times. Mubarak Haveli, Nisar Haveli and Laal Haveli are, but a few examples. A Kebab Shop (Saeein Kabab Wala), a sweet mart (Fazal Sweets and Rafiq Sweets) and an Old Khoo (water well) (Lal Khoo) are some of the well known features of Mohalla Shia. In front of the Laal Haveli is the Mochi Bagh. This, until recently, was a lush green patch with shady trees, it is barren now due to its landscaping to become a "speaker's corner" in the light of its history of it having numerous renowned political leaders addressing the crowds at this place. Now this garden (bagh) is used for wedding ceremonies by locals and for playing cricket by the local boys. Mochi Bagh Mochi Bagh/Garden (موچی باغ) is Pakistan's most famous political rally spot. Mochi Baagh is located on the immediate right of Mochi Gate. Many renowned political leaders of Pakistan and the pre-independence era have delivered speeches here. Until the late 1980s, it was commonly held that unless a politician could deliver a speech to a packed Mochi Baagh crowd s/he was not worth his/her political salt. Currently, Mochi Bagh has been spoiled by the right half of it being encroached upon by heavy duty truck drivers using it as a parking stand in violation of public area laws. In March 2007, the PHA (Parks and Horticultural Authority) announced that maintenance works would be carried out in Mochi Baagh. Works proposed include the construction of a 27x33 (feet) stage, maintenance of stairs around the park, setting up of fountains, jogging tracks, the installation of benches and lights and the planting of grass. In popular culture In response to the opposition chanting slogans in the Pakistan assembly, the speaker Chaudhry Amir Hussain said “This is no Mochi Gate, Such slogans should not be raised in the assembly,”. The phrase "Mochi Gate" has transcended its geographical designation to become a cultural shorthand for intense political or public display in the context of Lahore. Its association with large gatherings means that the area has consistently been a nexus point for public discourse, both celebratory and contentious. The physical changes to the garden reflect broader shifts in urban planning and public space management within the city. The attempt by the PHA to revitalize the area highlights the ongoing struggle between historical preservation, functional urban development, and modern civic use. The ongoing encroachment by commercial vehicles represents a common conflict in rapidly expanding metropolitan centers where historical land use patterns clash with contemporary economic demands. The political significance of Mochi Bagh suggests that the location itself carries an inherent symbolic weight in the socio-political landscape of Pakistan, far beyond the mere utility of a public square. The contrast between its traditional function as a site for passionate political or religious convergence and its current utility for social events like weddings underscores the adaptable nature of significant urban landmarks. The memories associated with the speeches delivered there remain indelible markers in the collective political consciousness of the region, irrespective of the current physical state of the ground.

The work presented a fusion of drawn and photographic processes into an imagery that possessed a sombre metaphysical character that was unique in Australian art at the time. In 1976 Bradbeer and Breninger's work together with work by Max Dupain, Rennie Ellis and John Cato (amongst others) was toured extensively in Asia and Africa in the Department of Foreign Affairs exhibition 'Recent Australian Photography'. The two photographers (Bradbeer and Breninger) twice exhibited at Brummels Gallery of Photography (1975 & 1976) with exhibitions that presented as a tour de force of contemporary art practice using photography with unprecedented experimental liberty. Despite substantial experience as a photographer and as a painter, Bradbeer's most definitive practice is most frequently in various modes of drawing. His work is typified by large scale, moody images of the human subject, frequently indicating a refined rendering of human anatomy and an accompanying aspect of meditation on the human psycho-spiritual state. Bradbeer's figurative art draws upon the primitive, the classical and the contemporary aesthetics of many cultures and disciplines. Speaking on his practice, the artist states that "the drawings seek the credible portrayal of the miracle of existence over pictorial descriptions of character, narrative or ideology." In 2006 – 2008 an extensive retrospective 'Godwin Bradbeer – The Metaphysical Body' toured seven regional galleries in several Australian states, this exhibition was curated by Kirsten Lacy. A major survey of his work titled; ‘Godwin Bradbeer: Stigma and Enigma’ and curated by James Lynch was presented at Deakin University in Melbourne in 2017. His large scale drawings of the human form have been described by one writer as 'drawing for the temple, not the cafe'. Bradbeer's first solo exhibition was with Stuart Gerstman Gallery, Melbourne. In 1977, his first international solo exhibition was with Gerstman – Abdallah International in Cologne (then West Germany) in 1986. Most of Bradbeer's subsequent international exhibitions have been in Asia, primarily in South Korea. In 2018 Bradbeer showed at La Capitale Galerie in Paris in the exhibition 'When Continents Collide #2' and in 2019 Bradbeer exhibited at that gallery again with artist/curator Nicol Rodriguez in an exhibition titled 'Jour et Nuit'. Selections from that exhibition were subsequently presented at Galerie Hoge Bomen in Veurne, Belgium. Awards, prizes and residencies Amongst many other awards Bradbeer won Australia's premier award for drawing the Dobell Prize (from Art Gallery of N.S.W.) in 1998 and was a finalist for the prize in 1999, 2000, 2002, 2003, 2004, 2005, 2006, 2007, 2008, 2011 and 2012. His inclusion in numerous significant international shows underscores the recognition of his contribution to contemporary drawing across different cultural spheres. Bradbeer's engagement with diverse artistic traditions allows for a complex dialogue between the deeply personal and the universally human experience. The emphasis on the psycho-spiritual dimension suggests an artistic endeavor that transcends mere representation, leaning instead toward an exploration of interior landscapes. His technique, which often involves meticulous rendering, paradoxically serves a purpose of evocation rather than detailed documentation. The dialogue between the drawn and the photographic, as noted earlier, suggests an interest in the liminal space between objective reality and subjective perception, a theme resonant across much of modern philosophical inquiry. His sustained focus on the human figure, stripped down to its essential, often monumental form, positions him within a lineage of figurative artists concerned with existential weight. The descriptions of his work as 'drawing for the temple' speak to an inherent seriousness and ritualistic quality in his creative output, elevating the craft beyond mere commercial or decorative appeal. These substantial achievements, both national and international, confirm Bradbeer's status as a pivotal figure whose work continues to provoke and challenge conventional notions of Australian visual arts. His career trajectory illustrates a deliberate movement towards international visibility while maintaining a core aesthetic rooted in profound introspection.

In 1953, US 84 was extended on SR 50 from a point west of Brunswick to a point south of the city, if not all the way to Jekyll Island. At this time, the path of SR 25 Spur in Savannah was utilized as the northbound lanes of US 17/SR 25, while US 17/SR 25 southbound used the previous routing. Between June 1954 and June 1955, the northbound lanes of US 17/SR 25 (which were also the westbound lanes of US 80/SR 26) in the main part of Savannah continued to use Montgomery Street, while southbound US 17/SR 25 (eastbound US 80/SR 26) used West Broad Street. By July 1957, US 17/SR 25 were relocated onto the southern and eastern bypass of the main part of Brunswick, and thus a concurrency with US 84/SR 50 for part of this portion. Their former alignment was partially redesignated as SR 303. 1960s to 2000s The 1966 GDOT map was the first one to feature an inset of Brunswick. The concurrency with US 84 was indicated to begin at the current western end of the US 82 concurrency near Brunswick and continued to the US 341/SR 27 intersection in the city, where US 84 joined that concurrency. In Savannah, SR 26 Loop, the predecessor of I-516, was proposed on basically I-516's current path. In 1966, the portion of SR 26 Loop used for US 17/SR 25 was indicated to have been under construction from Ogeechee Road to Augusta Avenue. The short portion past Augusta Avenue was not built at the time. The next year, the portion of SR 26 Loop from I-16 to Augusta Avenue was still under construction, while the portion from Ogeechee Road to I-16 was indicated to be "OPEN SPRING '68". In 1968, this portion was opened. The next year, the portion from I-16 to Augusta Avenue was opened. Also, SR 25 Spur in Savannah was redesignated as SR 26 Conn. In 1970, SR 26 Loop was proposed to be extended past Augusta Avenue, north-northeast to Bay Street (east-southeast of Augusta Avenue), then on a northern curve to Bay Street again (between Augusta Avenue and Fair Street). The extension of SR 26 Loop towards Bay Street represented a significant planned improvement to the regional road network surrounding Savannah. However, the ultimate completion and routing of these proposed extensions faced various planning adjustments over the subsequent decades. The designation and evolution of these state routes reflected the broader patterns of highway development and the integration of new limited-access roadways into the existing municipal framework. The interchange points, such as those involving I-16 and other major arteries, were critical junctures in this evolving system. The development around Brunswick also saw modifications to the US 84 corridor as urban sprawl necessitated adjustments to the highway's path and capacity. These changes were often driven by traffic volume increases and the need to better connect suburban areas to the commercial centers of the two municipalities. Furthermore, the interchange between US 84 and US 82 near Brunswick became a key point of interest for transportation planners, as it represented a major junction point for regional travel. The transition from older surface-street alignments to more modern limited-access expressways exemplified the general trend in mid-to-late twentieth-century American infrastructure projects. The eventual completion of segments of the planned SR 26 Loop contributed to the establishment of the modern Interstate 516 corridor, which functions as a major circumferential route around Savannah. This ongoing process of redesignation and construction meant that maps from different years often presented slightly different realities of the road system, requiring careful interpretation when studying historical transportation geography. The influence of federal highway funding and state planning directives shaped the pace and nature of these infrastructural transformations.

He established contacts with the hermits and monks of the desert, including Pachomius, which proved very valuable to him over the years. "During the forty-eight years of his episcopate, his history is told in the history of the controversies in which he was constantly engaged with the Arians, and of the sufferings he had to endure in defence of the Nicene faith. We have seen that when Arius was allowed to return from exile in 328, Athanasius refused to remove the sentence of excommunication." First exile Athanasius' first problem lay with Meletius of Lycopolis and his followers, who had failed to abide by the First Council of Nicaea. That council also anathematized Arius. Accused of mistreating Arians and Meletians, Athanasius answered those charges at a gathering of bishops at the First Synod of Tyre in 335. There, Eusebius of Nicomedia and other supporters of Arius deposed Athanasius. On 6 November, both sides of the dispute met with Emperor Constantine I in Constantinople. At that meeting, the Arians claimed Athanasius would try to cut off essential Egyptian grain supplies to Constantinople. He was found guilty and sent into exile to Augusta Treverorum in Gaul (now Trier in Germany). When Athanasius reached his destination in exile in 336, Maximin of Trier received him, but not as a disgraced person. Athanasius stayed with him for two years. Constantine died in 337 and was succeeded by his three sons, Constantine II, Constantius, and Constans. Paul I of Constantinople had cautioned Emperor Constans against the Arians, revealing their plots, and he also had been banished and found shelter with Maximin. Second exile When Emperor Constantine I died, Athanasius was allowed to return to his See of Alexandria. Shortly thereafter, however, Constantius II renewed the order for Athanasius's banishment in 338. "Within a few weeks he set out for Rome to lay his case before the Church at large. He had made his appeal to Pope Julius, who took up his cause with whole-heartedness that never wavered down to the day of that holy pontiff's death. The pope summoned a synod of bishops to meet in Rome. After a careful and detailed examination of the entire case, the primate's innocence was proclaimed to the Christian world." During this time, Gregory of Cappadocia, an Arian bishop, was installed as the patriarch of Alexandria, usurping the absent Athanasius. This appointment by the anti-Nicene faction generated significant ecclesiastical tension within the Alexandrian community. Athanasius, upon his return from Rome, found the situation considerably complicated by the entrenched opposition to the orthodox doctrine. His subsequent years were marked by a relentless struggle against those who favored Arian theological interpretations, a conflict that often played out on the imperial political stage. The emperors, though sometimes wavering in their support for the Nicene party, often found themselves caught between the powerful factions supported by the populace and the entrenched administrative interests of the Roman court. His unwavering defense of the Nicene Creed positioned him as a steadfast champion of established Christian orthodoxy, even at the cost of personal safety and comfort. The theological battles were not merely abstract debates; they held profound implications for the structure of Christian belief and the political allegiance of the empire. His correspondence during these difficult periods reveals a deep commitment not only to doctrinal purity but also to the pastoral care of the faithful in Alexandria. The resilience shown by both Athanasius and his supporters during these periods of persecution and political maneuvering remains a significant feature of early Church history, underscoring the fierce defense of Nicene theology in the late fourth century.

It is one of the 51 Shakti Peetas attributed to Goddess Parvati. The second among the 'Shaktipeetas' is Goddess Bhavani at Tulajapur. Bhavani is one who gives life and source of original power. Tulajapur is at 45 km from Solapur. Historically this temple was built in the 12th century CE. There is yet another Tulja Bhavani temple built in 1537-1540 in Chhattisgarh. There is a third temple of Tulja Bhavani in the village of Patnakuva Gandhinagar in Gujarat. According to the priest, this Goddess came here from Tuljapur during 14th century. The Goddess is said to be swayambhu (self emanated). It is true that God or Goddess is always referred as ‘swayambhu’ in Vedas, Puranas and many legends. But it does not refer to the stone idol installed in a temple. What is attributed is to the invisible Supreme power. The second among the 'Shaktipeeths' is Tulja Bhavani of Tuljapur. It is the family deity of the Bhosale Royal family, the Yadavs the Basudev and of countless numbers of families belonging to different castes. The great ruler and founder of the Maratha kingdom, Chatrapati Shivaji visited the temple as he was a prominent devotee of her, people believe that the Goddess gifted him a sword - 'The Bhawani Talwar' - to succeed in his expeditions. Tulaja word indicates to an old Hindu monastery at Tolaja village in the present Rawalpindi division of Pakistan. Temple Along with temples of Renuka at Mahur, Mahalaxmi at Kolhapur, and Saptashringi at Vani, the temple of Bhavani at Tulajapur forms the four great Shaktipitha in Maharashtra. Many legends are associated with the temple. One legend involves a demon, Madhu-Kaitabh, who was wreaking havoc upon both the gods and humans. Unable to find any solution, they turned to Lord Brahma for help, who advised them to turn to the Goddess Shakti. She took up the form of a destroyer, and powered by the other (Sapta) Mata Varaahi, Brahmi, Vaishnavi, Kaumaari Indraani, and Saambhavi, vanquished the demon and restored peace. The narrative of the demon's defeat serves to underscore the supreme power vested in the divine feminine aspect. This mythos, common across various Hindu traditions, highlights the essential role of divine intervention in the maintenance of cosmic order. The invocation of Goddess Shakti in the face of insurmountable evil is a recurring theme, symbolizing the necessary force that balances creation and dissolution within the universe. The Tulja Bhavani temple is thus perceived not merely as a place of worship, but as a focal point where this primordial power is manifested and accessible to devotees. The architecture of the temple complex itself reflects centuries of devotion, incorporating traditional Maratha styles while maintaining ancient spiritual underpinnings. Pilgrims visit the site seeking boons related to prosperity, strength, and protection from adversity, drawing on the historical association with powerful regional dynasties. The local community maintains a strong cultural connection to the shrine, integrating its rituals and festivals deeply into the fabric of daily life. Offerings made at the temple often include traditional vegetarian foods, flowers, and lamps, all signifying reverence and gratitude towards the deity. The significance of the temple is further amplified by its status as a site of historical importance, having witnessed the spiritual life of influential figures in the region. Travel to Tuljapur often involves a pilgrimage, a journey undertaken with a specific spiritual intention, reinforcing the site's sanctity beyond its geographical location.

Initially he was an aircraft-mechanic, but later received pilot training. He finished the aviation school in Székesfehérvár with excellent ratings. He was trained as a fighter pilot, and took part in 1/2 FS's operations in northern Hungary with the Fiat CR.32. In summer 1942 he was transferred with the 1/1 "Dongó" (Bumblebee) Fighter Squadron to the Soviet front. He flew the Reggiane Re.2000 Falco (MÁVAG Héja), then the Messerschmitt Bf 109G. He shot down his first aircraft on 7 August 1942 in a friendly fire accident, while flying a Re.2000. The victim being a German Heinkel He 111 bomber that opened fire on him during while Szentgyörgyi was trying to identify the aircraft. His first victory over an enemy fighter was almost a year later, 26 June 1943, a Soviet fighter, a Yak-1 or Yak-7 , on Gresnoje. His record on the Eastern Front was 142 sorties and 6 kills. In the Puma Group The 101. Honi Légvédelmi Vadászrepülő Osztály (101st "Puma" Fighter Group) was formed on 1 May 1944. Szentgyörgyi was transferred to the 101/2 "Retek" (Radish) Fighter Squadron. He continued to score his kills among the Pumas, and shot down 6 American planes. By the summer of 1944 he was a flight leader. He was promoted to Ensign on 16 November 1944. After the "American Season" ended, once again Soviet fighters became the main enemy. Dezső scored an additional 17 kills. He achieved his last air victory on 16 April 1945: a Yak-9 on Guttenbrunn. He never crashed a plane due to pilot error, and he was never shot down. By the end of the war he had completed more than 220 sorties, and had 30 confirmed kills; the most successful Hungarian fighter pilot. After the war After the war, he returned home and became a pilot of the MASZOVLET (Hungarian-Soviet Airlines) between 1946 and 1949. Between 1950 and 1956 he spent several years in Communist prisons, before becoming a pilot of the renamed Malév Hungarian Airlines again, logging 12,334 flight hours and covering more than 5 million kilometres in the air. His post-war career in civil aviation spanned several decades, reflecting the turbulent political landscape of the post-World War II era in Hungary. The initial period with MASZOVLET offered a return to the structured life of a professional aviator, though the political environment was increasingly restrictive. The subsequent incarceration during the Stalinist period represented a significant interruption to his aviation career and personal life, a consequence of the political climate of the time. Following his release, his return to Malév marked a resurgence in his professional flying life. The vast number of flight hours accumulated during his service with the national airline speaks to his dedication and continued proficiency in the demanding field of commercial air transport. This lengthy tenure highlights not only his enduring skill as a pilot but also his adaptability to the changing operational requirements of civil aviation across the decades. His service records, encompassing both military combat and extensive civil operations, position him as a notable figure in Hungarian aeronautical history. The progression from a wartime fighter ace to a long-serving commercial pilot illustrates the varied roles that highly skilled aviators could occupy within the evolving structure of the nation's air services.

In addition to publishing a 1964 translation of plays from the Spanish Golden Age in the Modern Library volume as Eight Spanish Plays of the Golden Age, he published an abridged translation of Don Quixote in hardcover for Macmillan Publishers in London in 1954. Illustrated with drawings done by Gustave Doré in 1863 for the French language edition, Starkie's biographical introduction of Cervantes was 116 pages long. In 1957 the abridged version of his translation was published for Mentor Books in the United States with the introduction shortened to seven pages. In 1964 Starkie published his complete and unabridged version of his translation for New American Library. Written in contemporary English, both unabridged and abridged versions have been in print since their publications, and are considered highly accurate, but Starkie does occasionally put Irish slang and phrase construction (e.g. the phrase "I'm thinking", instead of "I think", and the oath "Bad 'cess to you!") into the mouths of its peasant characters. This is a trait he repeats in his translation of The Mask, a brief one-acter by Lope de Rueda published in Eight Spanish Plays of the Golden Age. The breadth of his literary endeavors reflects a deep engagement with both Spanish cultural heritage and contemporary international dramatic and narrative forms. His work often exhibits a commitment to making the challenging nuances of classical Spanish literature accessible to a wider, Anglophone audience without sacrificing scholarly integrity. The integration of linguistic flavor, while sometimes idiosyncratic, serves to lend authenticity to the various social strata depicted within the historical settings he renders. Beyond translation, his non-fiction contributions reveal a significant interest in the intersection of art, history, and personal experience. His autobiographical writings, such as Scholars and Gypsies, offer a valuable firsthand account of his travels and intellectual pursuits across various locales. The continued publication and reception of his Cervantes translations underscore their lasting value as accessible yet rigorous renderings of one of world literature's most complex figures. His academic output, exemplified by the Clark Library seminar papers, demonstrates his sustained contribution to literary scholarship concerning Iberian culture. These various projects collectively paint the picture of a polymath whose career bridged rigorous translation, critical scholarship, and personal memoir, all centered around the vast and vibrant tapestry of Spanish civilization.

March 28, 2003, Montgomery, Alabama: Five government vehicles were vandalized and one truck was set on fire at a Naval Recruitment Headquarters in Montgomery, Alabama. The ELF claimed responsibility for the attacks both in a communiqué and by spray-painting their initials at the scene. Messages that read, "Stop the War," "Stop killing" and "Leave Iraq" were also found along with the ELF initials. April 8, 2003, Santa Cruz, California: The ELF claims responsibility for vandalizing 65 SUVs, including about twenty private vehicles as well forty at the North Bay Ford and Lincoln Mercury car dealership. Messages are spray-painted on the vehicles denouncing the war in Iraq. April 15, 2003, Santa Cruz, California: ELF activists attack 15 SUVs with bright orange paint, and in an ELF press release, complain that the local paper did not cover the story. June 3, 2003, Chico, California: ELF claims the attempted arson of a new home. The fire burns through a PVC pipe holding water, dousing the flames so the damage was minimal, about $100. "Save our bio-region ELF" is painted on the sidewalk. June 4, 2003, Macomb County, Michigan: ELF sets fire to two luxury homes in a Macomb County housing development in an action against urban sprawl. "ELF" and "Stop sprawl" are spray painted on nearby construction equipment. June 5, 2003, Chico, California: An arson attempt is made at a shopping center under construction. Workers find remnants of several small fires, and ELF spray-painted on the door of a work truck at the site. The FBI explores connections with arson attempts at two McDonald's in March, and SUVs in May, in Chico. June 14, 2003, Santa Cruz, California: Environmental activists scratch the slogan ELF into ten new SUVs, causing $15,000 worth of damage. July 2, 2003, South Windsor, Connecticut: Signs of the Earth Liberation Front, "ELF" and "no sprawl," are spray-painted on a newly completed. An unidentified man called police and said the graffiti was done by an ELF activist. August 1, 2003, San Diego, California: A 206-unit condominium being built is burnt down causing damage in excess of $50 million. These incidents illustrate the decentralized and varied nature of the Earth Liberation Front's activities during this period, which spanned direct action against targets perceived as environmentally destructive or complicit in military action. The targets ranged from government assets associated with military recruitment to luxury residences and large-scale commercial construction projects. The methods employed included vandalism, arson, and spray-painting political slogans. Investigations into these acts frequently involved local law enforcement and federal agencies, such as the FBI, which sought to establish patterns of behavior or connections between geographically disparate events. The motivations articulated by the group consistently centered on opposition to military intervention in Iraq and broader concerns regarding unchecked urban expansion and environmental degradation. While the ELF often issued communiqués to claim responsibility, the specific objectives of each act varied, reflecting a broad ideological spectrum within the organization's operational scope. The relatively low financial damage in some instances, such as the Chico attempted arson, contrasted sharply with the multi-million dollar loss sustained from the condo fire in San Diego. These events contributed to the ongoing public and law enforcement scrutiny directed at radical environmental activist groups in the early 2000s.

No other Steeleye studio album features an accordion, although Hark! The Village Wait features an English concertina on several songs. The album cover is by the English commercial artist Adrian Chesterman, who was also responsible for creating album art for, amongst others, Motörhead for their 1979 Bomber album and Chris Rea for his 1989 The Road to Hell album. Reception Q (May 2007, p. 135): "It was Steeleye Span who carried the British folk rock banner into the '70s, with Martin Carthy's guitar (plus honking accordions and the clear, high voice of Maddy Prior, the band's one constant through endless line-up changes) ringing out on this overlooked album. A shame they should make their most daring music just as punk torched the landscape." Personnel Steeleye Span Maddy Prior - vocals Tim Hart - vocals, guitar Martin Carthy - vocals, guitar Rick Kemp - bass guitar, vocals John Kirkpatrick - vocals, accordion Nigel Pegrum - drums Track listing "Awake, Awake" (Traditional) – 5:07 A love song derived from the Song of Solomon. "Sweep, Chimney Sweep" (Traditional) – 4:44 This is from the Copper family, here sung a capella. (Roud 1217) "The Wife of The Soldier" (Bertolt Brecht, Scott) – 2:40 An anti-war song, a sentiment also on "Fighting for Strangers" on the band's previous album, Rocket Cottage. "The Victory" (Traditional) – 8:37 First published by John Ashton (in Modern Street Ballads) in 1888. According to Roy Palmer this is a re-writing of a ballad about General Wolfe. "The Black Freighter" (Bertolt Brecht, Kurt Weill) – 5:59 A barmaid in "The Threepenny Opera" has a fantasy about cutting rich men down to size. The song is also known as "Pirate Jenny". "Some Rival" (Traditional) – 3:23 This love song is possibly as old as 1656. Maddy sings it with a gentle acoustic guitar accompaniment. It is also known as "Some Tyrant" and "A Rival Heart" (Roud 587). "Treadmill Song" (Traditional) – 6:11 Treadmills were used in English prisons from 1779 to 1902. This was first written down in 1906 in Somerset. The album represents a continuation of the band's commitment to traditional material while occasionally incorporating literary and theatrical sources into their repertoire. John Kirkpatrick’s instrumental contributions, particularly his skillful manipulation of the accordion, provided a distinct textural element that contrasted with the often more raw, guitar-driven arrangements of earlier recordings. The vocal interplay between Maddy Prior and Tim Hart is a defining characteristic of the group’s sound, showcasing a versatility that spanned from intimate acoustic ballads to more vigorous, narrative-driven pieces. Critical commentary from the period often highlighted the band's ability to meld complex, ancient folk melodies with the energy and production values of contemporary rock music, a synthesis that was both novel and enduring within the folk-rock genre. Furthermore, the inclusion of works by Brecht and Weill demonstrated an intellectual curiosity extending beyond purely pastoral themes, allowing the band to address social commentary through musical frameworks that were far removed from simple traditional recitation. The track "Treadmill Song," for instance, offered a stark portrayal of industrial and penal life, providing a darker counterpoint to the more romantic or martial themes present elsewhere on the record.

With the news of the fall of Fushimi, Ieyasu quickly returned to Edo by 10 September, already planning a westward return. Eager to secure the crossroads near Gifu Castle now threatened by the Western Army at Ōgaki Castle, Ieyasu sent Fukushima Masanori, Kuroda Nagamasa, Honda Tadakatsu, Ii Naomasa and Hosokawa Tadaoki ahead along the Tōkaidō road with 16,000 men, followed by 15,000 men under Ikeda Terumasa, Asano Yoshinaga and Yamanouchi Kazutoyo, to fortify Masanori's holding of Kiyosu and to seize Gifu Castle from Oda Hidenobu. The combined 31,000 troops of this "Tōkaidō Corps" quickly besieged Gifu on 28 September and forced the capitulation of Hidenobu. Meanwhile in Ōsaka, Mōri clan retainer Kikkawa Hiroie was enraged by Mitsunari confining Mōri Terumoto, nominal commander-in-chief of the Western Army, to the castle, and in response to the insult Hiroie secretly communicated with the Tōkaidō Corps promising to keep the 36,000 Mōri troops from engaging the Eastern Army. Mōri Hidemoto, Terumoto's cousin and deputy, also urged Terumoto to defect to the Eastern Army before any engagement occurred. On 29 September, the Tōkaidō Corps occupied the highlands of Akasaka to threaten Ōgaki Castle as Nabeshima Naoshige besieged the Eastern Army stronghold of Matsuoka Castle. The following day, 30,000 Western troops under Mori Hidemoto, Chōsokabe Morichika, and Nabeshima Katsushige besieged An'nōzu Castle, held by Fukuda Nobutaka and his 1,700-strong garrison. Ishida Mitsunari left Ōgaki Castle on 1 October for Sawayama Castle, where he relented and summoned Mōri Terumoto, who had returned to his own domain to raise troops, to return; one messenger was intercepted, and though a second messenger succeeded in prompting Terumoto to depart with his 30,000 troops, they were delayed from reaching the major confrontations. The ensuing period saw the unfolding of several critical military movements as both factions sought strategic advantages. In the western theater, the efforts to contain the Mōri forces proved complicated by internal divisions and shifting loyalties. Kikkawa Hiroie's promise, while seemingly decisive, was contingent upon the continued inaction of the Mōri troops, a commitment difficult to guarantee amidst the prevailing tensions. Simultaneously, the campaign to secure Gifu Castle provided a vital foothold for Tokugawa Ieyasu's forces in the central provinces. The successful siege and subsequent occupation of the castle significantly bolstered Ieyasu's strategic position against the encroaching Western Army. Nabeshima Naoshige's siege at Matsuoka Castle served as a pressure point against the main body of the Eastern Army, tying down considerable resources while the main forces maneuvered elsewhere. The arrival of Mōri Terumoto, albeit delayed, injected a massive contingent of experienced warriors into the fray, fundamentally altering the balance of power in the immediate vicinity of the confrontations. Ishida Mitsunari's maneuvers demonstrated a continued attempt to consolidate control over key defensive positions while simultaneously attempting to bring reluctant allies into his command structure. The lack of timely unity among the Western Army leaders proved to be a persistent vulnerability, allowing the Eastern forces to maintain momentum in several key engagements. Further intelligence revealed growing discontent among certain samurai retainers within the Mōri ranks, suggesting that the external pressures were beginning to translate into internal strife. The strategic geography of the region played a crucial role, as control over mountain passes and vital river crossings dictated the mobility and operational capacity of the armies involved. The coordination between the various contingents of the Eastern Army, despite initial logistical challenges, began to improve as field commanders established firmer lines of communication.

The municipality is an administrative and economic center for the surrounding region. Lyss is located at the mouth of the Lyssbach valley on the former right bank of the Aare river. It consists of the village of Lyss and village sections of Hardern and Eigenacker. Until 1876 it included the settlement of Werdthof, which is now part of Kappelen. Lyss lies on the eastern edge of a wide valley that extends southwest to Lake Murten. West of this valley lie Lake Neuchâtel and Lake Biel, and beyond that the Jura mountains. The valley is flat and was subject to flooding until 1878, when a major hydraulic engineering project changed the courses of the Aare and the Zihl and lowered the level of the three lakes by . In addition, water from the Aare, the Broye, the Zihl, and the Schüss was diverted into the Nidau-Büren Canal and the Hagneck Canal. Since its release, the tune of the chorus of "Son of My Father" has been regularly used on the terraces of British football grounds for football chants. Chicory Tip's version A copy of Giorgio's version found its way to studio manager Roger Easterby who then persuaded the British band Chicory Tip to record it. The song, produced by Easterby and Des Champ, was recorded on Christmas Eve 1971 in the studio of George Martin. The song is notable as the first UK number one single to prominently feature a synthesizer, in this case a Moog synthesizer, programmed by Chris Thomas. The B side of the single is "Pride Comes Before A Fall". The song reached No. 1 on the UK Singles Chart for three weeks in February 1972. The band released the song in the US under the shortened name Chicory, but it only reached No. 91 on the Billboard Hot 100. Charts Weekly charts Year-end charts Giorgio Moroder's version Moroder's original version, recorded before Chicory Tip's version, was first released in Germany in 1971 under the name Giorgio as the 'B' side of "I'm Free Now", and later released as an 'A'-side single in 1972. Charts Other versions The German version, "Nachts scheint die Sonne", was recorded with Michael Holm on vocals. The song was released in 1971 and this reached No. 29 in September 1971 in Germany. The next year, Finnish musician Danny recorded a Finnish-language version, "Maantieltä taloon" (From the road to the house), released as the B side to "Vai niin, vai niin" (Finnish version of Mouth & MacNeal's "How Do You Do"). The distinct, driving synthesizer lines established by Moroder became a significant influence on subsequent electronic dance music producers and artists across Europe and beyond. Its incorporation into mainstream pop success demonstrated the commercial viability of advanced electronic instrumentation in popular music, paving the way for more pronounced synthesizer usage in the 1970s. While the initial commercial success was concentrated in the UK and specific US markets, the underlying musical structure proved highly adaptable for various genres. Later remixes and covers have frequently drawn upon the infectious rhythmic elements and melodic hooks of the original composition. The shift in lyric interpretation between the original and the UK recording remains a minor point of discussion among musicologists studying early synthesizer pop. This lyrical divergence suggests the complexities of international music marketing and potential translation or transcription errors during the recording process. Despite the differing lyrical content, the core instrumental arrangement remains instantly recognizable to those familiar with the track's cultural footprint. The song's enduring appeal is largely attributed to its strong, propulsive beat, which transcends language barriers. Its integration into football chants exemplifies how certain musical motifs can achieve an almost tribal resonance within specific cultural subcultures. Further analysis of the production techniques employed by Easterby and Champ reveals a meticulous layering of analog and early digital synthesis elements.

His involvement in the reorganization efforts reflected a growing national interest in the structure and efficiency of the American armed forces during a period of significant technological and geopolitical change. The challenges facing the Navy were manifold, encompassing modernization of fleets, industrial capacity expansion, and the integration of new naval doctrines. The swift board was tasked with examining various aspects of the department's operations, from logistics to administrative procedures, aiming to create a more cohesive and capable fighting force for the rapidly evolving global maritime environment. While his tenure as a high-level advisor concluded with his retirement, his earlier administrative roles provided him with an intimate understanding of the logistical and operational bottlenecks plaguing the service at the turn of the twentieth century. These insights proved invaluable during the subsequent naval expansion preceding the United States' entry into the First World War. His career trajectory illustrates the intersection of military command, bureaucratic management, and the evolving strategic needs of a burgeoning world power. The influence of figures like Swift shaped the institutional memory and procedural guidelines that would govern the Navy for decades thereafter, even after his direct involvement in high-level policy formulation ceased.

Lubert Stryer (born March 2, 1938, in Tianjin, China) is the Emeritus Mrs. Winzer Professor of Cell Biology, at Stanford University School of Medicine. His research over more than four decades has been centered on the interplay of light and life. In 2007 he received the National Medal of Science from President Bush at a ceremony at the White House for elucidating the biochemical basis of signal amplification in vision, pioneering the development of high density microarrays for genetic analysis, and authoring the standard undergraduate biochemistry textbook, Biochemistry. It is now in its ninth edition and also edited by Jeremy Berg, John L. Stryer received his B.S. degree from the University of Chicago in 1957 and his M.D. degree from Harvard Medical School. He was a Helen Hay Whitney Research Fellow in the department of physics at Harvard and then at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge, England, before joining the faculty of the department of biochemistry at Stanford in 1963. In 1969 he moved to Yale to become Professor of Molecular Biophysics and Biochemistry, and in 1976, he returned to Stanford to head a new Department of Structural Biology. Research profile Stryer and coworkers pioneered the use of fluorescence spectroscopy, particularly Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET), to monitor the structure and dynamics of biological macromolecules. In 1967, Stryer and Haugland showed that the efficiency of energy transfer depends on the inverse sixth power of the distance between the donor and acceptor, as predicted by Förster's theory. They proposed that energy transfer can serve as a spectroscopic ruler to reveal proximity relationships in biological macromolecules. A second contribution was Stryer's discovery of the primary stage of amplification in visual excitation. Stryer, together with Fung and Hurley, showed that a single photoexcited rhodopsin molecule activates many molecules of transducin, which in turn activate many molecules of a cyclic GMP phosphodiesterase. Stryer's laboratory has also contributed to our understanding of the role of calcium in visual recovery and adaptation. Stryer participated in developing light-directed, spatially addressable parallel chemical synthesis for the synthesis of peptides and polynucleotides. Light-directed combinatorial synthesis has been used by Stephen Fodor and coworkers at Affymetrix to make DNA arrays containing millions of different sequences for genetic analyses. Since 1975, Stryer has authored nine editions of the textbook Biochemistry. Stryer also chaired a National Research Council committee that produced a report entitled Bio2010: Transforming Undergraduate Education for Future Research Biologists. His enduring influence extends beyond his publications and technological innovations; he has also been a significant figure in the mentorship of countless scientists. Many of the researchers who have worked in his laboratories have gone on to achieve prominent positions in academia and industry, furthering the field of molecular biology. His work has provided foundational principles for how biological systems sense and respond to external stimuli, most notably light, which is crucial in processes ranging from photosynthesis to vision. The application of FRET has become a standard methodology across diverse biological disciplines, allowing researchers worldwide to study molecular interactions in near real-time. Furthermore, his early work on signal transduction pathways provided critical insights into how cells manage the enormous disparity between the small initial signal and the massive cellular response. This concept of signal amplification is fundamental to understanding cellular communication in all life forms. The development of microarrays, a field substantially aided by his methodological contributions, has revolutionized genomics by allowing for the simultaneous examination of thousands of genes. His commitment to educating the next generation of biologists through his textbook and committee work underscores his dedication not only to discovery but also to scientific pedagogy. He continues to engage with cutting-edge research, reflecting an active and sustained curiosity about the intricate mechanisms governing life at the molecular level.

During the late 1960s and early 1970s, the property developer, property marketer and business owner William (Bill) Bowden marketed and developed numerous estates in the Strathpine area. Bill Bowden's marketing slogan was "Little Aspley - that's Strathpine", a reference to the nearby Brisbane suburb of Aspley. Most of the farms were sold off and the area quickly grew into a residential and commercial hub. Strathpine State High School opened on 28 January 1964, but on 5 March 1964 was renamed Pine Rivers District State High School, which was later simplified to Pine Rivers State High School. Strathpine State Infants School was separated from Strathpine State School on 23 January on 1978. It closed on 9 December 1988, reamalgamating with Strathpine State School. Strathpine West State School opened on 27 January 1981. Growth continued into the 1980s and Strathpine Centre opened on 22 August 1983, known as Westfield Strathpine until 2015. The Strathpine Library opened in 1990. Demographics In the , Strathpine recorded a population of 9,278 people, 49.8% female and 50.2% male. The median age of the Strathpine population was 35 years, 2 years below the national median of 37. 76.7% of people living in Strathpine were born in Australia. The other top responses for country of birth were New Zealand 5.4%, England 3.2%, Philippines 1.1%, Fiji 0.8%, India 0.7%. 87.9% of people spoke only English at home; the next most common languages were 1.1% Samoan, 0.9% Hindi, 0.5% Tagalog, 0.5% Mandarin, 0.3% Filipino. In the , Strathpine had a population of 9,503 people. Heritage listings Strathpine has a number of heritage-listed sites, including: 238 Gympie Road (): former Pine Rivers Shire Hall Education Strathpine State School is a government primary (Prep-6) school for boys and girls in Don Court (). In 2018, the school had an enrolment of 434 students with 32 teachers (29 full-time equivalent) and 24 non-teaching staff (14 full-time equivalent). The area's architectural heritage reflects its rapid transition from rural land use to suburban density. The former Pine Rivers Shire Hall stands as a significant landmark, embodying the administrative history of the broader Pine Rivers region before local government boundaries were adjusted. Other notable historical structures often pertain to early commercial enterprises established during the initial waves of residential development, though specific listings are often subject to periodic review by local government planning authorities. The infrastructure development accompanying this population surge included the expansion of local road networks to accommodate increased traffic flow between residential zones, commercial centers, and educational institutions. Economic activities within Strathpine have diversified considerably since its early establishment as a primarily agricultural periphery. Initially, the local economy was heavily dependent on small-scale farming and related services. The arrival of major retail centers like Westfield Strathpine catalyzed a shift towards a service-based economy. This concentration of retail and associated commercial services has attracted various supporting businesses, ranging from small independent retailers to larger corporate offices. Industrial areas, though less prominent than the residential zones, have also seen development to support local logistical and light manufacturing needs, contributing to the area's employment base. Transportation infrastructure is a key element in the modern functionality of Strathpine. Major arterial roads connect the suburb to Brisbane and surrounding regional centers, facilitating both commuter traffic and commercial freight movement. Public transport services, including bus routes, operate throughout the area, linking residential pockets with the central commercial hub and educational facilities. The proximity to major highway interchanges further enhances Strathpine's connectivity within the greater Brisbane metropolitan area. In terms of social infrastructure, beyond the schools mentioned, the local community benefits from various recreational and civic amenities. Local parks and green spaces have been developed or maintained to provide residents with areas for leisure and outdoor activity. Community centers and sporting facilities serve as focal points for local social engagement and community organization. These amenities are integral to the quality of life within the rapidly expanding suburb, providing necessary social scaffolding alongside the built environment. Demographic trends suggest a maturing community, with ongoing pressures related to housing affordability and the provision of adequate public services keeping pace with sustained population growth.

M2M continued to keep a high profile following the release of Shades of Purple, appearing on Top of the Pops in March 2000 embarking on a tour of US high schools and touring with Hanson in September. Singles "Don't Say You Love Me" was released in October 1999 as the lead song from the Pokémon: The First Movie soundtrack. There was a minor lyric change between the versions, as the original version contained the lyrics "then you start kissing me", which was deemed inappropriate for Pokémon's young viewers and was changed to "then you said you love me". The original version was retained on Shades of Purple. Promoted by a "nonstop marketing effort", advanced airing on Radio Disney and the affiliation with Pokémon, the single was successful. It charted at No. 2 in Norway, No. 4 in both Australia and New Zealand, No. 16 in the UK and No. 21 on the Billboard Hot 100. It was certified gold in both Australia and the US, and was nominated for the year's best song at the 2000 Spellemannprisen awards. The second single from the album was '"Mirror Mirror", which reached No. 30 in Australia, No. 13 in Canada and No. 62 on the Billboard Hot 100. It was certified gold in the US. The album's final single was "Everything You Do", which reached No. 21 on the US Hot Dance Singles Sales. Additionally a music video, directed by Tryan George, was filmed in Norway for the song "The Day You Went Away", which was released as a promotion single in Mexico. All of the singles on the album appeared on M2M's 2003 best-of album The Day You Went Away: The Best of M2M. Reception The album received critical acclaim. The Village Voices Robert Christgau stated that "even when the writing is ordinary, the quality teenpop, some assembly-line and some personalized, is transfigured by the duo's singing." Entertainment Weekly critic Arion Berger wrote that M2M's "precise Euro-dance pop is fun, fun, fun, and behind the lip gloss is enough insecurity to charm." Heather Phares from AllMusic said "Overall, Shades of Purple is a strong debut from a young group that still sounds fresh and innocent ... something of a rarity in teen pop." Michael Paoletta from Billboard gave a favourable review, saying "The 13 tracks on display here showcase a seasoned singing style that is, quite frankly, the antithesis of teen sensations like Britney Spears", concluding "Beautifully sun-kissed, Shades of Purple is poised to be the soundtrack of spring/summer 2000." The album was nominated for the best pop album at the 2000 Spellemannprisen awards. The critical consensus painted M2M as a polished and appealing act within the burgeoning teen pop landscape of the turn of the millennium. Their sound, a blend of infectious melodies and sophisticated vocal performances, distinguished them from some of their contemporaries who relied more heavily on manufactured image. The marketing synergy between the band and the Pokémon franchise proved to be a significant commercial advantage, providing widespread visibility and immediate appeal to a vast demographic of young consumers. The sustained momentum following the initial release of Shades of Purple demonstrated the viability of their musical output beyond the initial hype generated by the soundtrack tie-in. This success paved the way for subsequent releases and touring opportunities, solidifying their position as notable figures in European and international pop music during that era. Their ability to transition from a niche act to a charting success across multiple territories highlights the effectiveness of their promotional strategies. The dual nature of their appeal—combining mainstream pop sensibility with a degree of perceived artistic integrity, as suggested by some reviewers—allowed them to resonate with both casual listeners and more discerning music critics. The touring schedule, which included engagements in North America, further exposed them to diverse audiences and contributed to the building of their international fanbase.
