The application of unique, often whimsical, nicknames, such as 'The Pig' or 'Pimple face', suggests a close relationship between the railway crews and the machinery they operated, transforming utilitarian equipment into recognizable figures within the industry's community. These visual identifiers, whether official paint schemes or unofficial monikers, help document the varied life cycles of these mechanical assets.

The biosphere (which is technically a spherical shell) is virtually a closed system with regard to matter, with minimal inputs and outputs. Regarding energy, it is an open system, with photosynthesis capturing solar energy at a rate of around 100 terawatts. By the most general biophysiological definition, the biosphere is the global ecological system integrating all living beings and their relationships, including their interaction with the elements of the lithosphere, cryosphere, hydrosphere, and atmosphere. The biosphere is postulated to have evolved, beginning with a process of biopoiesis (life created naturally from matter, such as simple organic compounds) or biogenesis (life created from living matter), at least some 3.5 billion years ago. In a general sense, biospheres are any closed, self-regulating systems containing ecosystems. This includes artificial biospheres such as and , and potentially ones on other planets or moons. Origin and use of the term The term "biosphere" was coined in 1875 by geologist Eduard Suess, who defined it as the place on Earth's surface where life dwells. While the concept has a geological origin, it is an indication of the effect of both Charles Darwin and Matthew F. Maury on the Earth sciences. The biosphere's ecological context comes from the 1920s (see Vladimir I. Vernadsky), preceding the 1935 introduction of the term "ecosystem" by Sir Arthur Tansley (see ecology history). Vernadsky defined ecology as the science of the biosphere. It is an interdisciplinary concept for integrating astronomy, geophysics, meteorology, biogeography, evolution, geology, geochemistry, hydrology and, generally speaking, all life and Earth sciences. Narrow definition Geochemists define the biosphere as being the total sum of living organisms (the "biomass" or "biota" as referred to by biologists and ecologists). In this sense, the biosphere is but one of four separate components of the geochemical model, the other three being geosphere, hydrosphere, and atmosphere. When these four component spheres are combined into one system, it is known as the ecosphere. This term was coined during the 1960s and encompasses both biological and physical components of the planet. The Second International Conference on Closed Life Systems defined biospherics as the science and technology of analogs and models of Earth's biosphere; i.e., artificial Earth-like biospheres. Others may include the creation of artificial non-Earth biospheres—for example, human-centered biospheres or a native Martian biosphere—as part of the topic of biospherics. The study of biospheres is inherently complex due to the scale and interconnectedness of the systems involved, necessitating models and simplifications for scientific tractability. Early theoretical models often focused on global biogeochemical cycles, particularly the cycling of carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus, as these elements serve as the primary chemical conduits linking the biotic and abiotic realms. The maintenance of these cycles is fundamental to the stability of the biosphere; disruptions, whether anthropogenic or natural, can lead to large-scale alterations in atmospheric composition or terrestrial productivity. The concept of resilience within the biosphere refers to its capacity to absorb disturbances while retaining essentially the same function, structure, and feedbacks. Thresholds exist beyond which these systems may shift into entirely different, often less hospitable, stable states, a phenomenon central to discussions on planetary boundaries. Advances in remote sensing and global climate modeling have provided increasingly detailed spatial and temporal data on biosphere processes, allowing researchers to track changes in vegetation distribution, ocean productivity, and carbon sequestration capabilities across the globe. Furthermore, the functional diversity of the biosphere—the variety of roles and interactions organisms perform—is recognized as a critical determinant of ecosystem stability and resistance to invasion or collapse. Understanding the interplay between these functional traits and the physical constraints imposed by the geosphere and hydrosphere remains a major focus of contemporary Earth system science.

As the national governing body, Fencing Ireland also takes responsibility for running two of the largest events in the Irish calendar: the National Championships and the Irish Open. In 2006, the Irish Open was designated an FIE Satellite World Cup for the Men's Épée discipline. The lure of world ranking points has brought some of the biggest names in international fencing to compete in Dublin. History Fencing has been included in the Olympic Games since their modern-day inception in 1896 and the contemporary sport formally came to Ireland ten years later in 1906, when the Irish Fencing Club was founded in Dublin. It was not the first club in Ireland, but it was the first in which the principal aim was exercise and sport rather than duelling. The club closed in 1917, but was restarted again in 1933 following advertisements in Dublin newspapers. This was followed in 1934 by the Cork Fencing Club (renamed Club Palestrina in 1943) and the British Legion Fencing Club in 1935. In 1936 the Irish Amateur Fencing Federation was set up as the governing body of the sport in Ireland and in revised form remains the sole governing body of the sport in the country today. Clubs In the years following the establishment of the federation, clubs were set up at: Blackrock College Dublin University (1936, revived in 1940) The Royal College of Surgeons (1942) Kilkenny (1942) Limerick Fencing Club (1944) Shannon Fencing Club (1947) Salle d'Armes Duffy (1952) Cork County (1952) Clonmel (1954) UCD Fencing Club (1955) Pembroke Fencing Club, Dublin (2001) Salle Dublin (2005) Boyne Valley Fencing Club, Drogheda (2010) Fence Fit, Dublin (2011) - reopened as Ravenwood FC in Drimnagh Connaught Fencing Club, Tuam (2012) Blessington Fencing Club, County Wicklow (2012) Munster Blades (2013) in Nenagh, Limerick and Kilkenny Dundalk Fencing Club (2015) Brian Boru Fencing Academy, Abbotstown (2016) Mr. These clubs contribute significantly to the development of fencing talent across the island, providing competitive environments and training grounds for athletes of varying skill levels. The diversity in geographic location and institutional backing reflects the sport's growing penetration into various communities throughout Ireland. Modern fencing in the country sees participation not only at the elite international level, which is supported by the National Championships and the Irish Open, but also through grassroots programs aimed at introducing the sport to younger participants. These initiatives are crucial for ensuring a sustainable pipeline of future competitors. The evolution from early duelling societies to modern, sport-focused clubs mirrors the broader international shift in the practice of fencing, moving away from its historical combative roots toward a formalized athletic discipline. Coaching standards and training methodologies have also undergone considerable refinement since the early days of the Irish Fencing Club. Contemporary training often incorporates periodization, sports science principles, and specialized technical instruction tailored to the demands of modern Olympic competition in foil, épée, and sabre. Furthermore, the integration of technology, such as electronic scoring equipment, has standardized competition across all levels, allowing for precise and impartial judging of bouts. The relationship between the national governing body and the constituent clubs is symbiotic; the clubs provide the local infrastructure and athlete base, while the federation provides the competitive framework, administrative oversight, and international representation. This collaborative structure is vital for Ireland's continued participation and success on the global fencing circuit. Regional competitions and provincial qualifiers serve as necessary stepping stones between club training sessions and the main national events, allowing athletes to gauge their progress against peers from different localities before facing the highest levels of national competition. The commitment of volunteers and dedicated coaches, often operating within the framework of these established clubs, forms the backbone of the sport's operation in the country.

Dracula stands as the zenith of his literary career, yet the seeds of its atmosphere and characterization can be traced through his earlier, less overtly macabre writings. The posthumous publication of Seven Golden Buttons highlights the breadth of his creative output, encompassing material that may have existed outside the conventional published canon of his major novels. Scholarly editions, such as Bram Stoker's Notes for Dracula, provide invaluable primary source material for modern critics and biographers seeking to understand the genesis of his most famous creation. Upon his arrival at the butte Doc gives McQueen lessons on how to perform a powerslide. With his lessons complete, McQueen heads to Flo's V8 Cafe, where he meets four new racers; two from England and two from Mexico. These characters challenge McQueen to exhibition races throughout the story. With his first exhibition race completed McQueen participates in some tractor tipping with Mater before heading to his first Piston Cup race at Palm Mile Speedway, which he wins. Upon returning to Radiator Springs he participates in off-road training with Sarge. Fillmore also provides McQueen with a new organic fuel, which provides him with the ability to boost for short periods. He participates in a few more exhibition races in town before traveling to and winning his second Piston Cup race, this time at Speedway of the South. McQueen returns to Radiator Springs that evening. He is met by Mater, who teaches him the how to drive backwards, a skill that allows him to fill his boost. Through a race challenge from Sheriff he is introduced to nearby Ornament Valley, where he encounters three additional casual racers from Queens, New York. There he is also introduced to the Rustbucket Race-O-Rama, an arena event consisting of rusty vehicles. Lightning participates in multiple races in Ornament Valley before heading to his third Piston Cup seasonal race at Sun Valley International Raceway. When McQueen returns from his third victory he encounters the Delinquent Road Hazards trio, the tuner gang seen antagonizing Mack in the first film. The three challenge McQueen to a race through an abandoned mine, which they lose. Later Sally goes on a drive to the Wheel Well Motel, and McQueen is subsequently introduced to the Tailfin Pass area. Here he takes place in additional races and minigames in order to train for his final few Piston Cup races. Additionally McQueen participates in a monster truck race after being temporarily modified into a monster truck himself. Lightning and Mack head to the penultimate Piston Cup race at Smasherville International Speedway, but during the trip the Delinquent Road Hazards harass Mack and steals several of McQueen's parts. They are apprehended and McQueen learns that they were hired by Chick Hicks, McQueen's rival Piston Cup racer. McQueen wins his fourth Piston Cup race after confronting Hicks, who denies being involved. McQueen challenges Hicks to a four-race competition, with one race in each open-world environment, and the final race being the Piston Cup finale at Las Angeles International Speedway. This multi-race showdown against Chick Hicks proved to be a defining moment in McQueen's racing career, forcing him to utilize all the skills and allies he had gathered throughout the journey. The various settings of the competition tested his adaptability, from the dusty outskirts to the polished confines of the finale track. Throughout the trials, he refined his powerslide, maximized the efficiency of Fillmore's fuel, and utilized the unique maneuver of driving in reverse to charge his boost. His relationship with Mater evolved from a simple friendship to a crucial partnership, with Mater often providing unexpected tactical assistance during challenging races. The encounter with the Delinquent Road Hazards, though initially a source of conflict, served to sharpen McQueen's resolve and highlighted the persistent interference of his primary competitor. The rivalry with Hicks, however, transcended mere competition; it became a narrative of integrity versus ruthlessness. In the final race at Las Angeles International Speedway, the pressure was immense, with both drivers pushing their vehicles to their absolute limits. McQueen managed to maintain a strategic advantage, overcoming the aggressive driving style of Hicks in the closing moments. His victory in this culminating event cemented his status as a true champion, not just a fast racer. The triumph brought a sense of accomplishment that extended beyond the checkered flag, signifying a maturation in his approach to racing and life. Radiator Springs remained the steadfast heart of his adventures, a safe haven where his mechanical and personal growth was consistently supported by his community of friends.

Submission to the Neo-Assyrian Empire Warpalawas II was mentioned in the records of the Neo-Assyrian Empire under the name of Urpalla as one of five kings who offered tribute to Tiglath-Pileser III in 738 and 737 BC, and he appears to have maintained a policy of cooperating with the Neo-Assyrian Empire. Warpalawas II's pro-Assyrian orientation is visible in how how monuments used an Assyrianising style of sculpture: the best known of these monuments is a relief from Ivriz, on which Warpalawas II, himself represented in Assyrian style, is depicted praying to the Luwian Storm-god Tarḫunza. Relations with Tabal The king Wasusarma of the kingdom of Tabal claimed that Warpalawas II supported him in a battle where he defeated eight enemy kings near the city of Parzuta, although the veracity of Wasusarma's claim regarding the participation of Warpalawas in this battle as his ally is still uncertain. Vassals The kingdom of Tuwana was powerful enough to have included a sub-kingdom, located at the site corresponding to present-day Porsuk, and ruled by a king named Tarḫunazas who identified himself as a "servant" of Warpalawas II. Tarḫunazas himself recorded in his inscription that, in exchange for his services, Warpalawas II had rewarded him with Mount Muti, which was likely a rocky outcrop of the Taurus Mountains near the Cilician Gates. Relations with Phrygia Warpalawas II also carried out relations with the Phrygian kingdom to the north-west of Tuwana, as attested by a report from or by Aššur-šarru-uṣur, the Neo-Assyrian governor of Quwê, that Warpalawas II had demanded an audience with him in the company of an envoy of Midas II of Phrygia, with Aššur-šarru-uṣur being doubtful whether Warpalawas II was indeed loyal to the Neo-Assyrian Empire. This suggests that Warpalawas was one of the last still independent kings of the Tabal region who was being increasingly pressured by Phrygia and Assyria because of the location of his kingdom between these two powers. Some Old Phrygian inscriptions on basalt, possibly dated from Warpalawas II's reign, as well as the Phrygian robe depicted as worn by Warpalawas II in his Ivriz monument, suggest that aspects of Phrygian culture were arriving into Tuwana at this time. The presence of the name "Midas" on one of these inscriptions has led to the archaeologist M. Mellink hypothesising that this was the king Midas II of Phrygia, who had set up a monument in the city of his friend and ally, Warpalawas II. However, the long-time staunch pro-Assyrian orientation of Warpalawas II makes this hypothesis unlikely, and there is no evidence that Warpalawas II was ever an ally of Midas II. The strategic position of Tuwana allowed it to serve as a buffer state between the burgeoning influence of the Neo-Assyrian state and the expanding territories of Phrygia, a geographical reality that dictated the delicate political balancing act performed by its ruler. Archaeological findings within Tuwana reveal a complex tapestry of cultural influences, indicating that while centralized Assyrian authority was acknowledged, local traditions persisted and interacted with foreign imports. The religious iconography, as seen in the Ivriz relief, displays a synthesis of Mesopotamian imperial presentation with indigenous Luwian deities, a common feature among client states seeking to legitimize their rule under foreign suzerainty while retaining cultural identity. This syncretism underscores the pragmatic nature of the political relationships maintained by Warpalawas II. His dealings with neighboring powers, such as Tabal, were characterized by military alliances and mutual recognition of spheres of influence, even as the overarching shadow of the Assyrian military machine loomed over the entire region. The ambiguity surrounding the precise nature of his relationship with Midas II suggests that diplomatic interactions, even when documented, did not necessarily equate to formalized military or political allegiance, highlighting the fluid and opportunistic nature of ancient Near Eastern statecraft during periods of geopolitical flux.

Its highest point is Mount Welel. Towns and cities in West Welega include Dembidolo, Gimbi, Mendi, and Nejo. The Central Statistical Agency (CSA) reported that 40,606 tons of coffee were produced in West and East Welega combined in the year ending in 2005, based on inspection records from the Ethiopian Coffee and Tea authority. This represents 35.3% of the Region's output and 17.9% of Ethiopia's total output. Demographics Based on the 2007 Census conducted by the Central Statistical Agency of Ethiopia (CSA), this Zone has a total population of 1,350,415, of whom 671,538 are men and 678,877 women; with an area of 10,833.19 square kilometers, West Welega has a population density of 124.66. While 146,672 or 7.39% are urban inhabitants, a further 2,578 or 0.19% are pastoralists. A total of 266,773 households were counted in this Zone, which results in an average of 5.06 persons to a household, and 250,473 housing units. The three largest ethnic groups reported in West Welega were the Oromo (76.72%), the Mao (1.45%), and the Amhara (21.2%); all other ethnic groups made up 0.63% of the population. Oromo was spoken as a first language by 97.06%, 1.36% spoke Mao, and 21.15% Amharic; the remaining 0.43% spoke all other primary languages reported. The majority of the inhabitants professed Protestantism, with 54.55% of the population having reported they practiced that belief, while 24.19% of the population practiced Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity and 18.66% were Muslim. The 1994 national census reported a total population for this Zone of 1,547,075 in 289,555 households, of whom 766,461 were men and 780,614 women; 132,525 or 8.57% of its population were urban dwellers at the time. The three largest ethnic groups reported in West Welega were the Oromo (76.07%), the Amhara (22.4%), and the Mao (0.86%); all other ethnic groups made up 0.67% of the population. Oromo was spoken as a first language by 76.68%, 22.24% Amharic, and 0.67% spoke Mao; the remaining 0.41% spoke all other primary languages reported. Agricultural activities remain a cornerstone of the local economy, with coffee cultivation being the most significant cash crop. Beyond coffee, other agricultural products grown in the region include various grains, pulses, and horticultural items, which support both subsistence farming and local markets. The varied topography, ranging from fertile lowlands to the elevated slopes leading up to Mount Welel, contributes to the diverse range of agricultural practices employed by the inhabitants. Infrastructure development within the Zone has seen gradual improvements, with road networks connecting the major towns and facilitating the transport of agricultural goods to regional and national markets. Access to reliable energy sources and modern irrigation techniques remains a developing area requiring further investment to maximize agricultural potential. Education levels show a steady, though uneven, upward trend, with primary and secondary schools being present in most administrative centers. Healthcare provision is distributed through a network of health posts and larger health centers, although challenges persist in terms of specialist medical access and consistent supply of pharmaceuticals in more remote areas. The cultural landscape of West Welega is rich, characterized by diverse traditional practices intertwined with modern societal shifts influenced by national development policies. Traditional governance structures often interact with the formal administrative systems of the federal government, providing a complex social fabric to the region. Economic diversification efforts are underway to reduce reliance on the single dominant export commodity, though these initiatives are still in their nascent stages. Water resources management, particularly concerning rainfall patterns, is a critical environmental consideration influencing both agricultural planning and community survival in the region.

These genera represent a diverse group of insect taxa, exhibiting distinct biogeographic distributions across various continents and island chains. The distribution patterns suggest complex evolutionary histories influenced by geological events and climatic shifts. For instance, the presence of multiple species of Scaphioides across the Caribbean islands indicates a history of colonization and subsequent diversification in that insular environment. Similarly, the widespread occurrences of Silhouettella suggest a broader dispersal capability across different ecological zones, ranging from arid regions in Israel to more humid environments in Madagascar. The taxonomic revisions undertaken by Platnick and Dupérré have contributed significantly to the modern understanding of these groups, refining classifications based on detailed morphological and molecular evidence. The establishment of new species, such as those in Scaphioides and Scaphios, reflects ongoing systematic work to delineate species boundaries within these complex lineages. Further research employing advanced phylogenetic methods is likely to elucidate the precise relationships among these genera and to reconstruct the historical routes of their dispersal. The ecological roles of these species, although not detailed here, are presumed to be integral to the biodiversity maintenance within their respective habitats, playing roles as herbivores, detritivores, or predators, depending on their specific biology. The identification of types for each described species provides a stable reference point for future taxonomic studies and comparisons across different regional faunal surveys.

He played on the European Challenge Tour in 2002 and graduated to membership of the main European Tour in 2003. He won his first European Tour title at the 2004 Open de Madrid. In the 2007 European Tour, Sterne won at the Celtic Manor Wales Open, and finished second at the Johnnie Walker Classic, third at the BMW PGA Championship and fourth at the Barclays Scottish Open, therefore finishing 14th in the Order of Merit. In 2008 he picked up his third victory at the Joburg Open which is co-sanctioned by the Sunshine Tour, and at the end of 2008 won a further two European Tour tournaments in South Africa. His best year-end ranking on the European Order of Merit is 8th in 2013. His Celtic Manor win moved him into the top 40 of the Official World Golf Ranking for the first time. He has had six wins on the Sunshine Tour, and won that tour's Order of Merit in 2008. In January 2008 he reached a career high of number 29 in the Official World Golf Ranking. He missed most of the 2010 and 2011 seasons with injury. In February 2013, Sterne won the Joburg Open by seven strokes, to end a four-year winless drought from which he had been plagued with back injuries. This marked his sixth victory on both the European and Sunshine Tours and came on the back of a second-place finish he had in the previous week at the Dubai Desert Classic. It was also the first event that he had won wire-to-wire. The win moved him inside the top 60, which meant qualification for the WGC-Accenture Match Play Championship and to the top of the Race to Dubai standings. Later he finished second at the Alstom Open de France, ninth at the WGC-Bridgestone Invitational, 13th at the Omega European Masters, and 14th at the DP World Tour Championship, Dubai. As a result, he was eighth in the Race to Dubai final standings. During the 2014 season, Sterne finished fourth at the WGC-Cadillac Championship, 17th at the WGC-Accenture Match Play Championship and 35th at the PGA Championship. He qualified to the Web.com Tour Finals, where he ended second at the Nationwide Children's Hospital Championship. He finished ninth in the Web.com Tour Finals to earn his PGA Tour card for the 2014–15 season. Sterne is friends with South African golf icon, Gary Player, to whom he is often compared because of their similar small stature. His career trajectory reflects a sustained effort to maintain elite status across multiple international tours. The comparison to Gary Player often highlights a common characteristic in the golfers' physiques, despite differences in their playing styles and career peaks. While his triumphs on the European Tour are significant markers of his career, his success on the Sunshine Tour provided a crucial platform for development and consistent high-level performance in the Southern Hemisphere. The recurring theme of injury throughout his career underscores the physical demands of professional golf and the resilience required to return to competitive form. His 2013 resurgence was particularly notable, not only for the victory itself but for the sustained run of good play immediately preceding it, demonstrating a return to peak physical condition. His appearances in the WGC events further demonstrate his ability to compete against the world's leading golfers, although these events have often presented greater challenges than the standard European Tour schedule. The achievement of securing a PGA Tour card after the Web.com Tour Finals showcased his adaptability and competitive grit, allowing him to compete at the highest echelon of global golf for a period. His presence on the main tours solidified his reputation as a durable and competitive player, capable of achieving success across varied competitive environments.

Description C. virginianus is a moderately-sized quail, and is the only small galliform native to eastern North America. The bobwhite can range from in length with a wingspan. As indicated by body mass, weights increase in birds found further north, as corresponds to Bergmann's rule. In Mexico, northern bobwhites weigh from whereas in the north they average and large males can attain as much as . Among standard measurements, the wing chord is , the tail is the culmen is and the tarsus is . It has the typical chunky, rounded shape of a quail. The bill is short, curved and brown-black in color. This species is sexually dimorphic. Males have a white throat and brow stripe bordered by black. The overall rufous plumage has gray mottling on the wings, white scalloped stripes on the flanks, and black scallops on the whitish underparts. Females are similar but are duller overall and have a buff throat and brow without the black border. Both sexes have pale legs and feet. Distribution and habitat The northern bobwhite can be found year-round in agricultural fields, grassland, open woodland areas, roadsides and wood edges. Its range covers the southeastern quadrant of the United States from the Great Lakes and southern Minnesota east to New York State and southern Massachusetts, and extending west to southern Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma, Colorado front-range foothills to 7,000 feet, and all but westernmost Texas. It is absent from the southern tip of Florida (where the extinct Key West bobwhite subspecies once lived) and the highest elevations of the Appalachian Mountains, but occurs in eastern Mexico and in Cuba, and has been introduced to Hispaniola (both the Dominican Republic and Haiti), the Bahamas, the Turks and Caicos Islands, the U.S. Virgin Islands (formerly), Puerto Rico, France, China, Portugal, and Italy. Isolated populations also have been introduced in Oregon and Washington. The northern bobwhite has also been introduced to New Zealand. There is no self-sustaining population in Pennsylvania, where the bird is considered extirpated; it is also considered extirpated in the states of New Hampshire and Connecticut. Its distribution in New York has been limited to Suffolk and Nassau Counties on Long Island, as well as potential population pockets in Upstate New York. The bird is considered declining or extirpated throughout much of the Northeastern United States. Similarly, the bird is almost extirpated from Ontario (and Canada as a whole), with the only self-sustaining population confirmed to exist recorded on Walpole Island. Diet and Ecology The northern bobwhite is primarily an omnivorous ground feeder, subsisting on a diet composed of seeds, grains, insects, and various small invertebrates. These food sources are readily available in the diverse habitats it favors, allowing it to maintain a stable population across its wide geographic range. The quail exhibits a secretive and terrestrial lifestyle, spending the majority of its time foraging on the ground within dense cover. Its cryptic plumage provides effective camouflage against the varied backgrounds of grasslands and undergrowth, aiding in predator avoidance. During the breeding season, pairs establish territories within suitable cover, utilizing low shrubs and dense herbaceous vegetation for nesting sites. The nests are typically concealed on the ground, often camouflaged with surrounding debris. Parental care involves both parents incubating the eggs and subsequently tending to the chicks, which hatch in spring. The chicks are precocial, meaning they are relatively well-developed and mobile shortly after hatching, allowing them to begin foraging soon after emerging from the nest. Vocalizations play a significant role in social structure and territorial defense; the males possess a characteristic, loud call used for both attracting mates and establishing boundaries within their territory. Population trends suggest vulnerability due to habitat fragmentation and agricultural intensification across its core range. Conservation efforts are focused on maintaining suitable tracts of native grassland and edge habitats, particularly in the northeastern regions where its numbers have been notably reduced. The species generally responds well to management practices that promote a mosaic of agricultural and natural vegetation.

Pollination by non-flying mammals (therophily) The characteristics of the pollination syndrome associated with pollination by mammals which are not bats are: a yeasty odour; cryptic, drab, axillary, geoflorous flowers or inflorescences often obscured from sight; large and sturdy flowers, or grouped together as multi-flowered inflorescences; either sessile flowers or inflorescences or subtended by a short and stout peduncle or pedicel; bowl-shaped flowers or inflorescences; copious, sucrose-rich nectar usually produced during the night; tough and wiry styles; an adequate distance between the stigma and nectar to fit the rostrum of the pollinating animal; and potentially a winter–spring flowering period. Many non-flying mammals are nocturnal and have an acute sense of smell, so the plants tend not to have bright showy colours, but instead excrete a strong odour. These plants also tend to produce large amounts of pollen because mammals are larger than some other pollinators, and lack the precision smaller pollinators can achieve. The Western-Australian endemic Honey possum (Tarsipes rostratus) is an unusual non-flying mammal pollinator in that it has adapted to feeding exclusively on pollen and nectar. It is known to forage on a wide variety of plants (particularly in the families Proteaceae and Myrtaceae) including many with typical bird-pollinated flowers such as Calothamnus quadrifidus and many species of Banksia. Biology Pollination syndromes reflect convergent evolution towards forms (phenotypes) that limit the number of species of pollinators visiting the plant. They increase the functional specialization of the plant with regard to pollination, though this may not affect the ecological specialization (i.e. the number of species of pollinators within that functional group). They are responses to common selection pressures exerted by shared pollinators or abiotic pollen vectors, which generate correlations among traits. That is, if two distantly related plant species are both pollinated by nocturnal moths, for example, their flowers will converge on a form which is recognised by the moths (e.g. pale colour, sweet scent, nectar released at the base of a long tube, night-flowering). Advantages of specialization Efficiency of pollination: the rewards given to pollinators (commonly nectar or pollen or both, but sometimes oil, scents, resins, or wax) may be costly to produce. Nectar can be cheap, but pollen is generally expensive as it is relatively high in nitrogen compounds. Floral morphology and reward strategies are thus finely tuned to the sensory capabilities and feeding behaviors of the target animal. For therophilous interactions, the presence of a strong, often fermenting or musky scent serves as the primary long-distance attractant, replacing the visual signals prominent in insect-pollinated species. The physical structure of the flower must accommodate the morphology of the mammal, necessitating features like robust perianths capable of withstanding contact with a larger visitor. The positioning of the reproductive organs relative to the nectar guides the specific points of contact required for effective pollen transfer during the mammal's foraging routine. The longevity of the reward is also a factor; since mammal visitation may be less frequent than insect visitation, the plant must maintain a viable nectar or pollen supply over a longer period. Furthermore, the seasonal timing of flowering is often correlated with the activity patterns of the primary mammalian visitor, which in many temperate or arid zones are restricted to specific periods of the year. The development of highly specialized mutualisms, while efficient in terms of reproductive success for both parties, can sometimes create ecological vulnerabilities. If the specific pollinator population declines due to environmental changes or disease, the dependent plant species may suffer a dramatic reduction in reproductive output because alternative visitors may not possess the requisite behavioral or sensory adaptations to fulfill the pollination role. Conversely, a broad range of potential visitors, even if suboptimal, can provide a buffer against catastrophic pollination failure. The concept of functional group specialization is particularly relevant here, as it allows for a grouping of disparate species that share the same pollination mechanism, thereby facilitating broader ecological studies of pollination syndrome evolution across different biomes.

These diverse lines of inquiry encompass the taxonomic classification, evolutionary relationships, morphological adaptations, and ecological interactions of various Philippine Nepenthes species. Phylogenetic studies employing both plastid and nuclear markers have been instrumental in resolving the complex relationships within the Nepenthaceae and related families, providing a molecular framework for understanding the diversification of these carnivorous plants in the insular Southeast Asian environment. Morphological investigations have focused intently on the structure and development of the pitcher traps, which are central to the genus's predatory lifestyle. Specific attention has been paid to the complex chemical and physical properties of the pitchers, particularly the composition of epicuticular wax crystals, which play a critical role in creating a slippery surface to ensnare prey. Furthermore, biochemical analyses have elucidated the functional roles of enzymes present within the traps, such as acid endochitinase, which aids in the digestion and absorption of captured insects. Ecologically, research has moved beyond individual plant physiology to examine the broader trophic dynamics, investigating how the presence and efficiency of Nepenthes traps influence local and regional food web structures. These investigations collectively paint a detailed picture of the remarkable evolutionary trajectory and specialized biological mechanisms underpinning the success of these carnivorous flora within the unique biogeographic context of the Philippines.

Respekt is published weekly and has its headquarters in Prague. The New York Times describes Respekt as "influential." Several people involved with Respekt became influential in top level politics of Czechoslovakia and the Czech Republic; among them the first editor-in-chief Jan Ruml who served as the Minister of Interior between 1992 and 1997, Martin Fendrych (official at the Ministry of Interior) and (several ministerial position). Editors describe Respekt as "a liberal magazine which stands up for freedom of thought and the need of continuous questioning of its outcomes". The weekly concentrates on investigative journalism (often using information gleaned from police sources) and in-depth articles, and has been expanding to cover ecological activism and alternative culture movements in recent years. In 2005 Respekt published details about business connection between Prime Minister Stanislav Gross' wife and a brothel owner, starting a scandal leading to downfall of Gross several months later; in 2008 it published an article alleging that Milan Kundera, when a student, denounced to the police a Czech spy for the West.Milan Kundera demands apology from Respekt for defaming him The circulation of the weekly peaked at over 100,000 copies in the middle of the 1990s. At this time the (loss generating) weekly was bought by Karel Schwarzenberg´s R-Presse. The circulation has been dropping steadily over the time causing Respekt's losses to increase to 7 million Czk in 2003. In 2006 Zdeněk Bakala obtained majority in Respekt and planned to eliminate the loss by making the journal more mainstream. The proposed changes led to fear among both readers and the editors that the unique flavour of the weekly will be destroyed; in September 2006 all editors threatened to leave. Within a week the owners submitted to the pressure, recalled the manager responsible to implement the changes and brought in a new editor-in-chief, Martin M. Šimečka, former editor-in-chief of the Slovak daily SME. Modification of the visual style and the format was delayed until September 2007. The circulation in 2006 was around 25,000 copies and the weekly was read by approximately 80,000 people each week. In 2007 the circulation was around 16-17,000 copies. According to a February 2008 survey, it is read by 94,000 people and remains one of the most cited journals and newspapers in the Czech Republic. Legal actions Since Respekt regularly reports on its investigations into bribery scandals, criminal activity or government mishandling, legal action is periodically taken against Respekt, often by top level politicians. Most of these cases that have gone to court have been won by the weekly. The most visible case was the Czech government's 2001 attempt to sue Respekt for libel. The ability of Respekt to withstand numerous legal challenges underscores its perceived importance in the national discourse and its commitment to robust investigative reporting. These confrontations often highlight the tension between press freedom and the interests of powerful political and business figures within the Czech Republic. The consistent success of the publication in court suggests that its journalistic practices are generally seen by the judiciary as being within the bounds of legitimate freedom of expression, even when targeting high-profile individuals or state institutions. The editorial stance, consistently defined as liberal and critical, places the magazine in opposition to established power structures, a dynamic that fuels both its readership and its legal adversaries. Its ongoing relevance is tied to its capacity to function as a significant watchdog in the post-communist political landscape. The journalistic focus remains a blend of hard investigative pieces, which often uncover systemic corruption or ethical breaches, and cultural commentary that engages with contemporary social shifts. This dual focus allows it to maintain engagement across different segments of the educated public, preventing it from becoming solely a political organ, despite its frequent involvement in political controversies. The continuous struggle between its financial viability, dictated by circulation numbers, and its editorial imperative to pursue challenging stories defines the modern operational reality of the publication.

Flowering occurs from January to December and the follicles are elliptic, in heads of eighty or more, each follicle long, high and wide. Taxonomy and naming Banksia leptophylla was first formally described in 1981 by Alex George in the journal Nuytsia. George's description was based on Carl Meisner's Banksia pinifolia, an illegitimate name because the name had already been used by Salisbury for a different species. The lectotype was an earlier specimen collected by James Drummond. The specific epithet (leptophylla) is derived from the ancient Greek words leptos, meaning "fine" or "slender" and phyllon, meaning "a leaf". In 1988, George described two varieties of this species in the journal Nuytsia and the names are accepted by the Australian Plant Census: Banksia leptophylla A.S.George var. leptophylla that flowers in summer and autumn and has a perianth long; Banksia leptophylla var. melletica A.S.George that flowers in winter and has a shorter perianth than the autonym. Before Alex George's revision of 1981, this species was labelled informally as B. sphaerocarpa var. pinifolia or var. major. Distribution and habitat Variety leptophylla grows in shrubland and kwongan between Tathra National Park and Moora and var. melletica grows in kwongan near the coast between Kalbarri and Guilderton. Ecology Banksia leptophylla is one of five Banksia species, all closely related to B. sphaerocarpa, that have highly unusual flower nectar. Whereas other Banksia species produce nectar that is clear and watery, the nectar of these species is pale yellow initially, but gradually becomes darker and thicker, changing to a thick, olive-green mucilage within one to two days of secretion, and eventually becoming "an almost black, gelatinous lump adhering to the base of the flowers". It was first noted by Byron Lamont in 1980; he attributed it to cyanobacteria that feed off the nectar sugars. Noting that many of these cyanobacteria had heterocysts, he speculated that they aid the plant by fixing atmospheric nitrogen, which is then washed off the flower heads by rain, and absorbed by the proteoid root mat. This purported symbiosis was investigated by Barrett and Lamont in 1985, but no evidence of nitrogen fixing was found. Further investigation by Markey and Lamont in 1996 suggested that the discolouration is not caused by cyanobacteria or other microorganisms in the nectar, but is rather "a chemical phenomenon of plant origin". Their analyses indicated that the nectar had unusually high levels of sugar and free amino acids, but three of these species, including B. leptophylla, have since been shown to have normal nectar sugar compositions. The mechanism responsible for the unique nectar transformation remains an area of ongoing botanical research. Subsequent studies have focused on the interaction between specific phenolic compounds within the flower tissue and the sugars present in the nectar. Certain oxidation reactions, possibly catalyzed by enzymes present in the floral tissues, are hypothesized to be responsible for the progressive darkening and thickening of the exudate. The altered chemical structure likely results in the formation of complex polymers that give the nectar its characteristic gelatinous texture. This chemical change is theorized to be an adaptation related to pollinator attraction or seed dispersal, though the precise ecological function has not been conclusively determined. The morphology of the leaves on B. leptophylla, being notably slender, is consistent with the species name, suggesting a general adaptation to drier, open environments typical of kwongan heathlands. These habitats are characterized by poor, often nutrient-deficient soils, which places selective pressure on the flora to develop specialized survival mechanisms. The close relationship between B. leptophylla and B. sphaerocarpa underscores a recent evolutionary divergence within the genus, possibly driven by localized environmental pressures across the southwestern Australian landscape. Further genetic sequencing is being employed to map the precise phylogenetic relationship among the various Banksia species and their immediate relatives, offering greater insight into the evolutionary trajectory of these remarkable Australian natives.

In 1968, both undertakings merged to form the Rossendale Joint Transport Committee. Following local government reorganisation in April 1974, the boroughs were merged, along with nearby Bacup and Whitworth, forming the present-day Borough of Rossendale. In 1986, as part of the deregulation of bus services and to comply with the Transport Act 1985, the company's assets were transferred to a new legal entity. The company expanded over the following twenty years, operating local buses in Bury, Rochdale and Rossendale, as well as neighbouring Blackburn, Bolton, Burnley and Todmorden. In September 1990, a new depot was established in Rochdale, in order to support new routes introduced in the town following the deregulation of bus services. In September 2008, the company's main depot and office facilities were moved from Rawtenstall to Haslingden, with the former buildings subsequently demolished. In early 2009, concerns were raised about the council's intentions, in relation to their continued ownership of the company. It culminated in a public protest outside Rawtenstall Town Hall, with the aim of dissuading Rossendale Borough Council from selling. In July 2009, the council announced that it was retaining its ownership of the company, with an acceptable valuation not having been met by any potentially interested parties. In August 2013, the network was rebranded, with a new livery design of red, orange, yellow and white. At the same time, the company was renamed Rosso. Following the granting of approval on 20 December 2017, the company was sold by Rossendale Borough Council on 12 January 2018. The sale saw the company's 240 staff and 102 vehicles join Transdev Blazefield – a move which saw the investment of £3 million in a new fleet of high-specification vehicles for routes in and around Bury, Rochdale and Rossendale. In April 2018, the company's Haslingden depot, which opened ten years earlier, was closed. Staff and vehicles were reassigned within the business to nearby depots across Lancashire. Services and branding 464 The 464 service operates between Accrington and Rochdale via Rawtenstall up to every 15 minutes, with a half-hourly frequency during the evening and on Sunday. This route is operated by a fleet of Optare Versa single-deck vehicles branded in a two-tone purple and pink livery. The 464 service serves as a vital connection across several communities in the region, providing essential public transport links for residents commuting and accessing local amenities. Its consistent scheduling aims to cater to the varying travel needs throughout the day, ensuring accessibility for both daily commuters and leisure travellers alike. The use of Optare Versa vehicles indicates a commitment to modern, accessible transport solutions, featuring low-floor access suitable for passengers with reduced mobility. The distinctive purple and pink livery serves as a recognizable identifier for this specific route within the broader network structure. Operational efficiency on the 464 is maintained through careful scheduling, balancing the high-frequency daytime service with the reduced, yet reliable, evening and Sunday provision. This dual-frequency structure reflects the anticipated patterns of travel demand across the corridor linking Accrington and Rochdale. The route traverses varied urban and semi-rural landscapes, requiring drivers to navigate different traffic conditions and road types. Subsequent reviews of the service have focused on maintaining the current frequency while exploring opportunities for minor adjustments to improve passenger experience during peak travel times. The contract governing the operation of the 464 is subject to ongoing review by the relevant transport authorities to ensure it meets evolving local transport requirements.

On the night of February 16–17, 1962, Wilhelmsburg was widely flooded and seriously damaged by the North Sea flood. On March 1, 2008, Wilhelmsburg was transferred from the borough Harburg to the borough Hamburg-Mitte by a Hamburg law. Geography In 2006, according to the statistical office of Hamburg and Schleswig-Holstein, the quarter Wilhelmsburg has a total area of . Wihelmsburg borders in the north to the quarters Steinwerder, Kleiner Grasbrook and Veddel. In the east are the quarters Spadenland and Ochsenwerder of the Bergedorf borough. In the south are the quarters Neuland and Harburg of the Harburg borough and the state of Lower Saxony and in the east are the quarters Moorburg and Altenwerder of the Harburg borough. Demographics In 2006, Wilhelmsburg had 49,132 inhabitants. The population density was . 22.6% of the population were under the age of 18, and 14.6% were 65 years of age or older. 33.7% were resident aliens. 4,298 people were registered as unemployed. In 1999 there were 21,345 households, out of which 26.8% had children under the age of 18 living with them and 39.9% of all households were made up of individuals. The average household size was 2.18. Population by year In 2006, there were 7,204 criminal offences (147 crimes per 1,000 people). There were 8 elementary schools and 6 secondary schools in the quarter Wilhelmsburg and 52 physicians in private practice and 11 pharmacies. Economy Parts of the port of Hamburg are located in Wilhelmsburg. Infrastructure The hospital Wilhelmsburger Krankenhaus Groß Sand has 257 beds and a day care center for geriatrics. Transportation Wilhelmsburg is serviced by the rapid transit system of the city train with the Wilhelmsburg station. The islands of Wilhelmsburg, Steinwerder, Veddel and Kleiner Grasbrook are connected via numerous bridges. The main connections to other parts of Hamburg are the Hamburger Elbbrücken (Hamburg Elbe Bridges) which consist of the Norder- und Süderelbbrücken (Northern and Southern Elbe Bridges), that connect Wilhelmsburg with the City Center of Hamburg in the north and with the quarter of Harburg in the south, the Kattwyk-Bridge (world's largest vertical lift bridge) in the southwest and the Köhlbrand Bridge which is a major connection from Wilhelmsburg to the nearby motorway 7 and the New Elbe Tunnel in the northwest. According to the Department of Motor Vehicles (Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt), in the quarter Wilhelmsburg were 13,714 private cars registered (280 cars/1,000 people). Culture Since 2007, the music and art festival Dockville takes place every year in summer. The quarter also hosts various cultural institutions and community centers that cater to the diverse resident population. Educational facilities extend beyond the listed schools, encompassing vocational training centers and adult education programs that support continuous learning among inhabitants. Commercial activities are varied, ranging from local retail shops serving daily needs to specialized businesses catering to the maritime and industrial sectors present in the area. Residential areas feature a mix of older tenement buildings and more modern housing developments, reflecting the area's ongoing transformation and growth. The proximity to the port district contributes significantly to the local economic character, with many residents having employment connections to the shipping and logistics industries. Parks and recreational areas, though sometimes constrained by the urban density, provide necessary green spaces for residents. Efforts are continually underway by municipal planners to enhance the quality of life, focusing on improving public transport links and developing sustainable urban infrastructure. The relationship between the historical industrial past and the contemporary maritime and residential use defines much of the area's contemporary identity. Tourism, while not a primary driver, benefits from the unique atmosphere created by the convergence of industrial heritage and modern urban life, particularly during events like Dockville. Environmental considerations remain pertinent, especially concerning water management due to the quarter's location on the Elbe River and its susceptibility to tidal influences. The administration of the quarter involves collaboration between the local district government and various neighborhood associations representing the interests of the populace.

These scholarly works collectively trace the shifting paradigms surrounding the understanding of alcohol use disorder, moving from earlier descriptive or moralistic frameworks toward the biopsychosocial models prevalent in modern addiction science. The conceptualization of alcoholism as a progressive disease, championed notably by Jellinek, represented a significant departure from previous societal judgments, aligning the condition with other recognized chronic illnesses. This reframing necessitated a corresponding evolution in clinical approaches, shifting focus from punitive measures to treatment modalities aimed at managing a chronic condition. The research cited illustrates the intersection of quantitative data analysis, as seen in studies examining patient histories and drug efficacy, with qualitative shifts in medical understanding. The persistence of debate, however, is evidenced by contrasting perspectives, such as those questioning the very nature of the "disease" label itself, highlighting the complexity inherent in classifying human behavior within a medical context. The inclusion of articles discussing the placebo effect underscores the critical role of expectation and psychological factors in the manifestation of both the condition and its perceived treatments. Furthermore, the references to the official organ of Alcoholics Anonymous demonstrate the influence of self-help movements on the broader scientific discourse concerning substance dependency. The historical trajectory suggests a gradual institutionalization of addiction within psychiatric and medical spheres, a process fraught with both scientific advancement and cultural resistance. Modern pharmacological research continues to build upon this foundational conceptual shift, seeking biological markers and effective interventions for this complex disorder. The varying methodologies employed across these sources—from large-scale surveys to focused clinical trials—reflect the multidisciplinary nature required to fully comprehend the multifaceted pathology of alcohol use.

Initially associated with the political right, by 1943 Roy drifted towards the left under the influence of Louis Aragon and adhered to the French Communist Party, openly attacking fascism and Vichy sympathizers. He left the Communist Party after the suppression of the Hungarian Revolution of 1956 and, as a contributor to Le Nouvel Observateur, became a fixture on the anti-totalitarian left. He was a signatory to the Manifesto of the 121 in favor of Algerian independence. His literary output spanned a diverse range of forms, encompassing poetry, novels, essays, and short fiction. His early work reflected the social and political turbulence of the period, often employing surrealist or highly symbolic imagery to convey disillusionment or fervent idealism. The themes in his fiction frequently explored themes of exile, memory, and the complexities of human connection amidst societal upheaval. His engagement with the Algerian independence movement underscored his deep commitment to anti-colonial struggles and his evolving political conscience. Later in his career, while maintaining a critical distance from rigid ideological structures, his writings retained a profound lyrical quality, even in his more philosophical essays. Critics have noted the evolution of his style from the more overtly charged political poetry of his early years to a more nuanced, introspective prose later on. This shift suggests a move from public ideological declaration toward a more internalized examination of the human condition. He maintained a reputation as a poet deeply invested in the cultural landscape of France while simultaneously engaging with international political currents. His dedication to literary discourse was evident in his numerous essays defending the role and necessity of art in a changing world.

His first wife, Paula Rivera, died and became a widower but he later married Hilaria del Pilar (a sister of Marcelo H. del Pilar), on April 22, 1877. Like his brother in law, Arellano was an active Freemason, hailing from Logia Lusong No. 185. Buan was his masonic name. He also solicited funds for Filipino expatriates in Spain when del Pilar had to flee to Spain, because of allegedly subversive articles that appeared in the Filipino newspaper that del Pilar published, the Diariong Tagalog (Tagalog Newspaper). He was also part of the short-lived La Propaganda, a movement founded by his brother-in-law del Pilar and Mariano Ponce, which sought reforms in the political landscape of the Philippines. Membership in La Liga Filipina and Katipunan In 1892, Arellano and other freemasons, like Andrés Bonifacio, joined La Liga Filipina, which was founded by José Rizal upon his return to the country. Arellano was elected the league's secretary. A few days after the founding of La Liga Filipina, Rizal was arrested and detained in Fort Santiago and then later deported to Dapitan island in Mindanao. On July 7, 1892, it was Gov. Eulogio Despujol who announced Rizal's immediate deportation to Dapitan. On the same day, the Katipunan was founded at Arellano's home in 72 Azcarraga Street (now Claro M. Recto Avenue), Manila where Andres Bonifacio— a Liga member— assembled Teodoro Plata, Valentin Diaz, Ladislao Diwa, Jose Dizon and Arellano himself to establish the said underground association. Its main goal was to reach Philippine independence from Spain and not just reforms. During the undisclosed October 1892 meeting of the Katipunan, Arellano was elected the first president of its Supreme Council and the first to be given the title Supremo. During his term as president, he endorsed the Katipunan's laws developed by its members particularly Plata and Diwa. In February 1893, Bonifacio saw Arellano as ineffective in leading the secret organization, thus, Roman Basa replaced him and became the second Supremo. In spite of his removal as president, Arellano respectfully continued to be active in the movement. He organized provincial councils in Bulacan during the same time Bonifacio and other members also organized councils in Manila, as a result, they attained one of the goals of Rizal in forming the Liga. Later life and death Arellano brought back the Liga in April 1893 to keep up the efforts of Rizal, despite not being present with them. His efforts to revitalize the league were part of a broader commitment to the nationalist aspirations brewing among Filipinos throughout the late nineteenth century. The clandestine nature of the Katipunan necessitated a network of loyal and capable individuals, and Arellano’s organizational skills proved valuable even after his initial leadership role diminished. The political climate remained volatile, with Spanish authorities employing increasingly harsh measures against any organized dissent. This repression forced revolutionary activities further underground and necessitated the creation of more robust local structures to maintain the revolutionary momentum. His provincial work in Bulacan provided a vital regional foothold for the burgeoning independence movement, demonstrating the geographically dispersed nature of the resistance. The continued existence of these provincial councils underscored the desire among various sectors of Filipino society for self-determination, mirroring the reformist sentiments initially championed by La Propaganda. Despite the internal power struggles within the Katipunan, Arellano remained a steadfast advocate for the ultimate goal of sovereignty. His dedication to maintaining the organizational framework of the nationalist groups reflected a deep-seated conviction in the necessity of a unified struggle for a free Philippines. These activities placed him at the nexus of intellectual ferment, political agitation, and armed revolution, shaping him as a significant, if sometimes overlooked, figure in Philippine history.

The Senior squad Fifth and sixth form rowers. The senior squad is made up of the oldest rowers in the school and is the squad from which the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th VIIIs are selected. The senior squad travel to many head races and regattas throughout the year including the Armada Cup in Switzerland, the Schools' Head Of the River Race and The National Schools Regatta. Hampton Head The boat club hosts two rowing events each year in the head race season; Hampton Small Boats Head (the most popular head race of the year); and Hampton Fours and Eights Head. Each race is over the same distance of roughly 3 km, raced downstream from just below Sunbury Lock to the finish, roughly 50 metres downstream of Platts Eyot. Successes Hampton has produced three treble winning 1st VIIIs in its history: 1985, 1986 and 1988. In 2004 Hampton won 1st, 2nd and 3rd VIIIs at the Schools' Head of the River Race. In 2013, at the same race, they came first in the following categories; Championship VIII's, 2nd VIII's, 3rd VIII's, J16 Championship VIII's, J16 2nd VIII's, J15 2nd VIII's, and J15 3rd VIII's, winning a total of 63 gold medals. Many rowers from Hampton have also gone on to compete at international levels and in recent years Hamptonians have consistently competed for Oxford and Cambridge in the Boat Race; in 2003 two sets of Hamptonian brothers (James and David Livingston, Matthew and Ben Smith) competed. The rigorous training regimen demands commitment from all members, balancing the demands of academic schedules with intensive physical conditioning necessary for elite rowing performance. These squads train regularly on the local stretches of river, utilizing dedicated coaching staff who oversee technical aspects, fitness protocols, and race strategy. Participation in the internal selection processes for the senior squad is highly competitive, reflecting the high standards the club sets for its athletes. Beyond the competitive racing circuit, the club fosters a strong sense of community among its members. Social events and non-rowing activities help to build camaraderie, which is often cited by athletes as a crucial element in sustaining long-term dedication to the sport. Alumni connections remain a valuable resource, with former rowers often assisting with coaching, mentoring current students, or providing insight into the transition to university and professional rowing careers. The club’s infrastructure includes access to modern training equipment and appropriate berthing facilities on the river, supporting year-round training capability, although competitive racing is seasonally focused. The commitment shown by the current student body mirrors the dedication of those who have achieved great heights for the club in the past.

Edward Carmien is a fiction and non-fiction author and editor of science fiction, fantasy and other topics. He is professor of English at Mercer County Community College, New Jersey, where he teaches science fiction. Carmien is a member of the Science Fiction and Fantasy Writers of America (SFWA) and the Science Fiction Research Association (SFRA). The Cherryh Odyssey was compiled by Carmien to mark the thirtieth anniversary of the publication of Cherryh's first two novels in 1976, Gate of Ivrel and Brothers of Earth. An Author's Perspective" – by Jane Fancher "A Pioneer of the Mind" – by Betsy Wollheim "Oklahoma Launch" – by Bradley H. Cherryh's Fiction" – by Burton Raffel "A Great Deal in Sand: Hammerfall by C.J. Cherryh" – by John Clute "C.J. Cherryh: Is There Really Only One of Her?" – by Heather Stark "Shifting Ground: Subjectivities in Cherryh's Slavic Fantasy Trilogy" – by Janice Bogstad "The Human as Other in the Science Fiction Novels of C.J. Stinson "A Woman with a Mission; or, Why Vanye's Tale Is Morgaine's Saga" – by Janice C. Crosby "Of Emorys and Warricks: Self-Creation in Cyteen – by Susan Bernardo "Dr. Ariane Emory, Sr.: Psychopath—Or Savior?" – by Elizabeth Romey "The Literary Life of C.J. Cherryh" – by Edward Carmien "Selected Bibliography of C.J. Cherryh" – by Stan Szalewicz Synopsis The Cherryh Odyssey consists of eight analytical essays on C. Cherryh's works, four personal reflections, and a fifty-six page bibliography of Cherryh by Stan Szalewicz. Also included is a preface and a biography, "The Literary Life of C.J. Cherryh" by the editor, Edward Carmien. In "Introduction: What We Do for Love", science fiction author and scholar James Gunn explains how difficult it must have been for Cherryh to enter the male-dominated science fiction arena in the mid-1970s. Gunn discusses the challenges faced by women writers navigating a field predominantly populated by men during that era. The anthology serves as a significant retrospective, offering critical analysis of Cherryh's varied contributions to speculative fiction. The inclusion of multiple essays allows for a multifaceted examination of her thematic concerns and narrative structures across her diverse body of work. Different contributors focus on distinct aspects of her writing, ranging from her engagement with cultural identity to her exploration of complex psychological states within her characters. Janice Bogstad's essay, for example, delves into the subtleties of her Slavic Fantasy Trilogy, offering insight into how cultural frameworks inform her world-building and character development. Betsy Wollheim's piece, "A Pioneer of the Mind," likely addresses the intellectual rigor and innovative thinking present in her science fiction narratives. The compilation reflects a scholarly interest in how Cherryh utilizes science fiction tropes to explore profound human conditions. Her frequent engagement with themes of societal alienation, intercultural misunderstanding, and the nature of selfhood is a recurring motif analyzed throughout the volume. Burton Raffel’s essay on "A Great Deal in Sand: Hammerfall by C.J. Cherryh" focuses on a specific novel, dissecting its narrative mechanics and thematic resonance. The inclusion of critiques from established figures like John Clute lends weight to the critical assessment of her literary merit. The essay "C.J. Cherryh: Is There Really Only One of Her?" by Heather Stark prompts a discussion about the breadth and distinctiveness of her literary voice. The book also touches upon the personal and creative journey of the author. Edward Carmien’s own reflections offer an insider's view into the life and craft of Cherryh. Susan Bernardo’s analysis of Cyteen explores how the concept of self-creation functions within the narrative architecture of that specific series. Elizabeth Romey’s provocative essay, "Dr. Ariane Emory, Sr.: Psychopath—Or Savior?", highlights the ethical ambiguities that Cherryh frequently presents to her readers, challenging simplistic moral categorizations. Collectively, these essays map out a career marked by intellectual depth and stylistic versatility, positioning Cherryh as a major figure in contemporary science fiction literature. The sheer scope of the bibliography underscores the sustained interest in her oeuvre by the academic and fan communities.

Citations In 1907, an influential translator of the ancient Indian epic The Mahabharata, named Bhishagratna, argued that Suśruta was one of the sons of the ancient sage Vishvamitra. Bhisagratna also asserted that Sushruta was the name of the clan to which Vishvamitra belonged. In Chapter 7 of the five-volume History of Indian Medical Literature, published in 1999, physician-scholar Gerrit Jan Meulenbeld covers a variety of theories on Suśruta's identity and the Sushruta Samhita's publication history. The name Suśruta is listed as one of ten Himalayan sages in a treatise on medicinal garlic that was included in the sixth century CE Bower Manuscripts. Followers Sushruta attracted a number of disciples who were known as Saushrutas and required to study for six years before beginning hands-on surgical training. Before starting their training, they took a solemn oath to devote themselves to healing and to do no harm to others, often compared to Hippocratic Oath. After the students had been accepted by Sushruta, he would instruct them in surgical procedures by having them practice cutting on vegetables or dead animals to perfect the length and depth of an incision. Once students had proven themselves capable with vegetation, animal corpses, or with soft or rotting wood – and had carefully observed actual procedures on patients – they were then allowed to perform their own surgeries. These students were trained by their master in every aspect of the medical arts, including anatomy. Sushruta on medicine and physicians Sushruta wrote the Sushruta Samhita as an instruction manual for physicians to treat their patients holistically. Disease, he claimed (following the precepts of Charaka), was caused by imbalance in the body, and it was the physician's duty to help others maintain balance or to restore it if it had been lost. To this end, anyone who was engaged in the practice of medicine had to be balanced themselves. Sushruta describes the ideal medical practitioner, focusing on a nurse, in this way:That person alone is fit to nurse, or to attend the bedside of a patient, who is cool-headed and pleasant in his demeanor, does not speak ill of anyone, is strong and attentive to the requirements of the sick, and strictly and indefatigably follows the instructions of the physician. (I.34) Legacy Sushruta's medical prowess is exhibited through his writings on rhinoplasty, involving nasal reconstructions using skin from the patient's forehead or cheek, often for criminals punished with amputations. His meticulous descriptions of surgical techniques, including specialized instruments, remain remarkably advanced for their time. The Sushruta Samhita details numerous surgical procedures, many of which correlate with contemporary plastic surgery practices. Furthermore, the text provides extensive knowledge regarding different types of fractures and their appropriate methods of setting and treating them. Beyond surgery, the treatise covers aspects of ophthalmology, dentistry, and gynecology, demonstrating a broad scope of medical understanding. The text also discusses pharmacological preparations, outlining various herbal remedies and their correct dosage. Some scholars have pointed to the systematic nature of the Samhita as evidence of a highly organized medical tradition predating many classical European medical systems. The emphasis placed on preventative care and maintaining bodily equilibrium aligns with broader philosophical concepts prevalent in ancient Indian thought. Dissemination of this knowledge appears to have been achieved through oral tradition supplemented by written texts, ensuring its transmission across generations of practitioners. The detailed anatomical knowledge presented suggests extensive empirical observation and dissection, although the exact nature and frequency of such practices in the early centuries CE remain subjects of ongoing academic debate. The lasting impact of Suśruta's work is evident in the subsequent evolution of Ayurvedic medicine.

While Kira travels to Bajor to meet with her ex-lover Shakaar Edon, Odo visits Vic to inquire further. Vic observes that Odo clearly is in love with Kira, but is afraid to pursue her, whereas Kira likes him but considers him only a friend. Vic claims that Odo's biggest obstacle is his reserved, aloof personality, and suggests he needs to "have some fun". He has Odo perform on piano during one of Vic's shows, and then arranges a double date with a pair of holographic women. Odo begins to feel more relaxed in his day-to-day life. Later, Vic arranges an encounter with "Lola", a holographic singer made to look like Kira, but Odo is dissatisfied at her lack of Kira's personality, and knowing that he is only comfortable with her because he knows she's a hologram, becomes frustrated and leaves. Vic, determined to take matters into his own hands, invites Kira to dinner, supposedly on Odo's behalf. Vic then persuades Odo to come to the holosuite to see a "new and improved" Kira hologram. Odo and Kira share a romantic date and a dance at Vic's club, but when Vic reveals to Odo that his date is with the real Kira, not a hologram, Odo leaves, angered and embarrassed. The next day, Kira confronts Odo, insisting they need to discuss what happened over dinner, "anywhere but a holosuite". Odo asks whether Shakaar would object to that, believing she is still seeing him, but Kira tells him her trip was strictly business, and that she isn't romantically involved with anyone. Odo sarcastically asks, if they have dinner, whether she would also like a dance afterward, and a kiss; Kira heatedly responds that she might. Odo declares "Well, then, who needs dinner? Why don't I just get it over with and kiss you right now?" Kira replies, "Well, why don't you?" and Odo grabs her and kisses her passionately. Later, Odo stops by the Holodeck to thank Vic for his help. Production and casting Executive producer Ira Steven Behr had been intending since the fourth season of Deep Space Nine to introduce the character of a lounge singer who provided romantic advice to the main characters; the role had been offered to Frank Sinatra, Jr. and Steve Lawrence for potential scenes in the fourth and fifth seasons, but they had declined. In the sixth season, Behr decided that an entire 1960s-era Las Vegas–themed episode should be created, resulting in the production of this episode. This episode, titled "The Afterlife," is notable for its exploration of Odo's internal conflicts regarding emotional vulnerability and romantic connection. The intervention by Vic serves as a catalyst, pushing Odo out of his habitual stoicism and forcing him to confront his desires. Kira's initial resistance to Odo's advances is rooted in her professional detachment and the complexities of her relationship with Shakaar Edon, which provides a narrative counterpoint to the burgeoning chemistry between Odo and Kira. The rapid escalation from tentative interactions to a decisive kiss highlights the significant personal shift occurring within Odo's character arc throughout the season. Furthermore, the episode touches upon the thematic implications of artificiality versus genuine connection, particularly through the various holographic representations of Kira used by Vic. The production choices, such as the intentional incorporation of a Las Vegas aesthetic, were meant to provide a heightened, stylized backdrop for these intimate and emotionally fraught character moments, distinguishing them from the typical operational settings of Deep Space Nine. The successful resolution of the romantic tension between Odo and Kira marks a significant milestone in their relationship, altering the established dynamics within the station's ensemble cast.
